prs.title: fix: realtime Talk cuts off multi-sentence replies with playback-overflow
prs.body:
Closes #148658

## What Problem This Solves

Realtime Talk cuts off spoken replies that have multiple sentences partway through and cancels the turn with reason `playback-overflow`, even though the reply itself is properly formed and the provider is still delivering it normally.

## User Impact

On the web client, realtime voice replies with multiple sentences (Google Live and gateway-relay transports) now play to completion instead of being cancelled partway through a sentence. The native Android client uses a separate playout implementation (`RealtimePlayout.kt`) with its own bound and never sends `playback-overflow`, so this PR does not change Android behavior. No config, schema, or JSON output changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

`RealtimeTalkPcmOutputQueue` (shared by the web realtime Talk transports) rejects further audio when either of two limits trips: how many seconds are queued ahead of the `AudioContext` clock, or how many `AudioBufferSourceNode`s are still alive. Providers can relay an entire spoken reply far faster than it plays back, so both limits can be hit long before the reply finishes, and the transport cancels the whole turn.

There are two changes here, one per limit.

**Queued seconds: 10s to 60s.** A few sentences of audio commonly arrive in a second or two, so 10s left too little headroom for ordinary replies. 60s of 24kHz mono PCM16 is under 3MB.

**Source count: fixed 320 to derived 3,000.** The gateway relay re-chunks provider audio into 20ms frames (`RELAY_OUTPUT_AUDIO_FRAME_BYTES = 960` in `src/gateway/talk/relay/session-create.ts`), and each frame becomes one source that is only released on `ended`. 320 sources is therefore 6.4s of speech, so on gateway-relay the source cap trips first no matter what the seconds cap is. The seconds change alone would not have fixed relay sessions. The source cap is now `ceil(MAX_QUEUED_SECONDS / 0.02)`, the number of relay-sized frames the seconds budget holds, so the two limits stay coupled if the budget is retuned. It is still a hard bound on graph-node count for frames far smaller than the relay contract.

Thanks to @saariuslystoned for measuring the source-cap behavior and pointing out that the original test only ever reached the seconds gate.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config ui/vitest.config.ts ui/src/pages/chat/talk`: 21 files, 343 tests passing.
- New regression test that mirrors the relay's framing: 750 frames of 480 samples at 24kHz (15s of speech) while the mocked clock advances at 1/3.6 of real time. It failed on the previous commit with `overflow` and passes now. The earlier test (60 chunks of 250ms, from the issue's synthetic repro) is kept, but it only exercises the seconds limit.
- The tests that assumed 320 sources (`audio.test.ts`, `gateway-relay.test.ts`, `google-live.test.ts`) now expect 3,000.
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the four changed files: clean.

<details>
<summary>What was not run</summary>

- The playback tests use a mocked `AudioContext`. I have not run this in a real browser with real audio output, so the live microphone and speaker symptom from the issue is not reproduced here.
- `pnpm tsgo:ui` reports 5 errors in `src/infra/fs-safe-advanced.ts`, `src/wizard/clack-prompter.ts` and `ui/src/components/mcp-app-view.ts`. They look like stale dependencies in my checkout and appear with and without this change. Nothing under `ui/src/pages/chat/talk/` is affected.

</details>

prs.title: fix(memory): avoid owner errors for configured dreaming workspaces
prs.body:
Closes #149215

## What Problem This Solves

### Summary

Fixes an issue where dreaming workspace enumeration fails with `AgentSelectionRequiredError` in an explicit multi-agent configuration when the runtime primary workspace is already present in the configured roster, but no primary agent is repeated in the call.

## Why This Change Was Made

### Root Cause

`resolveMemoryDreamingWorkspaces` first collects configured workspace owners. Its final primary-workspace branch nevertheless resolves a default agent before checking whether that canonical workspace already exists. In an explicit fleet without a default owner, that unnecessary lookup throws.

### Changes

- Reuse a known canonical workspace entry when no primary agent association was requested.
- Normalize optional owner IDs before that decision, including empty/whitespace input.
- Continue adding explicitly supplied owner associations.
- Continue requiring an owner for an unknown primary workspace.
- Cover real paths, symlink aliases, nullable optional ownership, explicit associations, and unknown-workspace rejection.

## User Impact

Callers can include an already-configured runtime workspace without adding an ambient/default agent or repeating an owner the roster already records. Existing owner sets remain intact.

This is a narrow configuration-resolution repair related to #147157. It does not claim to resolve that report's separate long-running model call or fleet-wide starvation symptoms.

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof

Ran the supported built CLI through a small synthetic plugin that imports the public `openclaw/plugin-sdk/memory-core-host-status` API. Each run used a fresh real configuration file and five existing workspace directories, `agents.ownership: "explicit"`, no default/system agent, and no model or Gateway calls. The resolver was not mocked.

The command handler was:

```js
import { resolveMemoryDreamingWorkspaces } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/memory-core-host-status";

api.registerCli(({ program }) => {
  program.command("workspace-proof")
    .option("--agent <id>")
    .option("--primary-owner <id>")
    .action(options => {
      const rows = resolveMemoryDreamingWorkspaces(api.config, {
        primaryWorkspaceDir: api.config.agents.entries.primary.workspace,
        primaryAgentId: options.primaryOwner,
      });
      console.log({
        workspaceCount: rows.length,
        owners: rows.flatMap(row => row.agentIds).sort(),
      });
    });
}, { commands: ["workspace-proof"] });
```

Invocation: `pnpm openclaw workspace-proof --agent primary`.

| Source | Public SDK call | Observed result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main `ca7c90068054dae7378d9d3bef42f11823bc1212` | Roster-only control | Exit 0, five workspaces and the five configured owners |
| Same main | Already-configured primary workspace | Handler entered; `AgentSelectionRequiredError`; exit 1 |
| Intermediate fix `21f5d8196b5eb3c47562c79848a78f7197f756cd` | Whitespace-only primary owner | Handler entered; `AgentSelectionRequiredError`; exit 1 |
| Final repaired tree, committed as `45398ad44ce03a2bca697b6f5f479d0e75895898` | Same primary workspace call, owner omitted or whitespace-only | Both exit 0, five workspaces and unchanged owners |

Repaired CLI output:

```text
CLI_WORKSPACE_ENTERED
CLI_WORKSPACE_PROOF {"workspaceCount":5,"owners":["editor","ops","primary","research","reviewer"]}
CLI_PROOF_EXIT 0
```

The `--agent` option selects the CLI/plugin context; the fixture deliberately does not repeat that option as `primaryAgentId` in the SDK call. The configuration itself already owns the selected workspace.

### Test

- Red-first owner regression failed on the original implementation with `AgentSelectionRequiredError`.
- After merging current `main` (which removed lower-value cases from this file in #159120 and conflicted only on an adjacent test name): `pnpm test src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts` passed 15 tests.
- Changed test file cost: `pnpm test src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` reports 1.24 s in Vitest for 15 tests (tests 7%), or 6.9 s wall including pnpm and worker startup.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base upstream/main` passed on the earlier merged head. The current head `49378d9` merges current `main` again to pick up the Bun plugin retention fixture deflake (#160200) behind the last CI failure. On it, `pnpm test src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts` passes 15 tests and `pnpm tsgo:core` plus oxlint on the changed files pass; `check-changed` now stops at the env-var budget ratchet because current `main` itself is over budget (`OPENCLAW_*` 484 > 483 since `670415932ee`).
- `pnpm build`: passed before and after the repair.
- Formatting and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Independent Codex review through P2: no accepted/actionable findings.
- The first native Codex review found the normalized-empty ID gap; it was reproduced in both the regression and built CLI, fixed using the existing normalizer, and the staged final tree passed a fresh P2 review.
- Final `codex review --base origin/main`: `findings: []`, `patch is correct`, exit 0.

## Risk

- Ownership/compatibility: no new owner is inferred for an existing workspace. An explicit primary owner still adds its association; an unowned primary workspace in an explicit fleet still fails closed.
- Canonical paths: symlink aliases are checked against the same workspace identity used to build the roster map.
- No schema, storage-format, protocol, configuration-option, or model-inference changes.

## CI history and recovery

CI on the current head `49378d9`: `openclaw/ci-gate` fails only on two UI e2e shards, both outside this diff: `ui/src/e2e/chat-user-avatar-alignment.e2e.test.ts` and `ui/src/e2e/model-catalog-partial-refresh.e2e.test.ts`. The same tests also failed in 5 and 3, respectively, of 18 other PR CI runs sampled between 09:35 and 22:07 UTC on 2026-09-28. The history below covers earlier heads.

The first non-draft CI run is **not green**: [34996372730](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/34996372730) finished with 145 successful jobs, 17 skipped jobs, and five failed tooling shards plus the aggregate gate.

The failed files are `pr-main-refresh.test.ts`, `pr-operation-lock.test.ts`, `pr-merge-hosted.test.ts`, `pr-cross-checkout.test.ts`, and `pr-crabbox-merge-bypass.test.ts` under `test/scripts`. They fail on unhandled repository metadata queries such as:

```text
Unexpected GitHub operation: api --hostname github.com repos/fixture/repo -H Cache-Control: max-age=0
```

The CI merge checkout included main `0a64ea33db7ac4e060c9c9b4d9bd7b0a53d86a83`. That base contains #149230 (`7e8a52c3f76`), which changed `scripts/pr-lib/merge-outcome.sh` to request the authoritative repository identity and changed the locator JSON request. The surrounding test fixtures do not handle those calls. These tooling files are outside this PR's two-file diff.

I reproduced the same six `pr-cross-checkout` failures on a separate, unchanged latest-main checkout at `7bc9893a0818426f07c32293cc03ba81cb33df73`:

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run test/scripts/pr-cross-checkout.test.ts
# 6 failed | 4 passed; same Unexpected GitHub operation error
```

This is an observed main-baseline failure, not a flake claim or a green CI claim. No unrelated fixture edits, skipped tests, or relaxed checks have been added to this repair.

Upstream #149294 (`7dc8a1e79659afb833df4bbfe363744c8d775e5c`) repaired those fixtures. On clean main `40e6f12380e306c92c47e96f3d0caa8fe94fb825`, all five previously failing files now pass: **279 passed, 1 skipped**. This PR was rebased onto that verified main at `c6e53e4137135ab95b10de1827547b7da1b9343b`.

Both repair commits are patch-identical according to `git range-diff`, and both changed files are byte-identical to reviewed head `45398ad44ce03a2bca697b6f5f479d0e75895898`. The existing real CLI evidence therefore describes unchanged repair code. The rebased dreaming suite passes **21 tests**.

The new exact-head run [35007354698](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/35007354698) finished with **147 successful jobs, 17 skipped jobs, and three installation failures plus the aggregate gate**. The three jobs failed before tests while `@matrix-org/matrix-sdk-crypto-nodejs` downloaded its native artifact:

```text
Download Failed Error: Response status was 500
ReferenceError: err is not defined
Error: ERR_PNPM_EXECUTOR_LIFECYCLE_SCRIPT_FAILED
```

Affected jobs: `checks-node-compact-large-20`, `checks-node-compact-large-27`, and `checks-node-changed-extensions-config-2`. A failed-job-only rerun was requested with `gh run rerun ... --failed`, but GitHub rejected it with `Must have admin rights to Repository.` No second attempt started. This run remains red pending a maintainer-authorized retry; no dependency overrides or test suppression were added.

## Changelog

Release-note context: dreaming no longer rejects a runtime primary workspace whose configured owners are already known. No release-owned changelog file was edited.

## Notes

AI-assisted: yes. Fully tested for the workspace-resolution and built-CLI surface described above; no live dreaming/model run is claimed.

prs.title: fix(tasks): recompute terminal retention after lost-task recovery
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a task loses its backing session, maintenance marks it `lost` and stamps the
short 24-hour lost-window retention (`cleanupAfter = lostAt + 24h`). When the
durable ledger later records a real terminal result, maintenance recovers the task
to `succeeded`/`failed` but never recomputes `cleanupAfter`, so the recovered
record keeps `lostAt + 24h` instead of the standard 7-day terminal retention from
its actual `endedAt`. If recovery happens more than 24h after the lost-mark
(Gateway down overnight, long-running job), the recovered terminal record is
pruned on the very next sweep — the user never sees the recovered outcome,
defeating the recovery feature's purpose of preserving finished work across
Gateway restarts (#145940). Even on quick recovery, the record gets only the
remainder of the short lost window instead of the documented 7-day terminal
retention (#126063, #126095).

## Why This Change Was Made

The defect is in `applyTaskRecordPatch` (`src/tasks/task-registry-records.ts`),
the lifecycle owner that stamps `cleanupAfter` for terminal records: it only
recomputed when `cleanupAfter` was missing, so the numeric lost-window value
survived a `lost` → terminal transition. Recovery paths (`markTaskRecovered` /
`projectTaskRecovered` in `src/tasks/task-registry.maintenance.ts`) also
preserved the numeric value.

The fix recomputes the terminal retention whenever a terminal status is reached
from `lost`, and makes the `projectTaskRecovered` projection always recompute.
The invariant: the short lost-window retention applies only while the record is
still `lost`; once recovered, the standard terminal retention from the recovered
`endedAt` applies. Files changed: `src/tasks/task-registry-records.ts` and
`src/tasks/task-registry.maintenance.ts` (fix), `src/tasks/task-registry.store.test.ts`
and the `test/fixtures/task-registry-recovery-restart.ts` fixture (regression
tests). No new dependencies, configuration options, or schema changes.

## Review-followup fixes

- **Exclude unchanged `lost` status from the recovery predicate (P2).**
  `isTerminalTaskStatus("lost")` is true, so the recovery recompute also ran when
  a still-`lost` record received a metadata-only or cleanup-only update
  (e.g. `setTaskCleanupAfterById`), silently replacing the explicit deadline the
  retention owner honors with `endedAt + 24h`. The predicate now requires a
  *different* terminal status (`next.status !== "lost"`): only a real recovery
  recomputes, and a still-`lost` record keeps its existing deadline. A regression
  test ("preserves an explicit lost-task deadline on a cleanup-only update")
  covers this: it fails on the pre-fix predicate (deadline 45260000 replaced by
  88400000) and passes with the fix.
- **Prove persistence across real OS process restarts, not just reload (proof
  followup).** The previous proof reloaded the registry from SQLite inside one
  process, which is not independent proof of an operating-system process
  restart. The committed subprocess regression test now spawns the fixture as
  three genuinely separate OS processes (`node --import tsx`, distinct PIDs)
  sharing one SQLite state dir: seed → recover → verify, then the parent reloads
  and runs the next sweep. The corrected deadline demonstrably survives real
  process restarts, and the next sweep keeps the recovered record.

## User Impact

Recovered terminal cron tasks now keep the documented 7-day retention from their
recovered end time, so their outcome stays visible in task history instead of
being pruned shortly after recovery. Tasks that are never lost are unchanged;
`lost` records still use the 24-hour window (and still honor an earlier explicit
lost-task deadline).

## Evidence

- **OS-process-restart recovery proof (before/after).** The real task-registry
  module chain runs against one real SQLite state dir across three genuinely
  separate OS processes (each a distinct `node --import tsx` child), so
  persistence is proven across real process restarts — the same boundary a
  Gateway restart crosses — not just an in-process registry reload. A lost cron
  task whose 24h lost-window deadline has already expired is written by process
  1, recovered by process 2, and read + swept by process 3. Timestamps and PIDs
  are redacted below; each phase printed from a distinct process.

  **Before (pre-fix source):** recovery keeps the expired lost-window deadline,
  so the very next sweep prunes the recovered record (`pruned: 1`,
  `still-present: false`) — the recovered outcome is lost.

  ```
  [seed]    seeded lost task: status=lost cleanupAfter=... (2026-09-17T05:41:39.953Z) expired=true
  [recover] reload saw: status=lost cleanupAfter=... stale-expired=true
  [recover] recovered: status=succeeded cleanupAfter=... corrected-in-future=false corrected=false
  [sweep]   reload saw: status=succeeded cleanupAfter=... preserved-across-restart=false
  [sweep]   sweep: maintenance={"reconciled":0,"recovered":0,"cleanupStamped":0,"pruned":1} still-present=false
  ```

  **After (fixed source):** recovery restores the standard 7-day terminal
  retention from the recovered `endedAt`; the corrected deadline survives all
  three process restarts and the next sweep keeps the record
  (`pruned: 0`, `still-present: true`).

  ```
  [seed]    seeded lost task: status=lost cleanupAfter=... (2026-09-17T05:42:28.485Z) expired=true
  [recover] reload saw: status=lost cleanupAfter=... stale-expired=true
  [recover] recovered: status=succeeded cleanupAfter=... (2026-09-23T15:42:38.378Z) corrected-in-future=true corrected=true
  [sweep]   reload saw: status=succeeded cleanupAfter=... preserved-across-restart=true
  [sweep]   sweep: maintenance={"reconciled":0,"recovered":0,"cleanupStamped":0,"pruned":0} still-present=true
  ```

  `RESULT: PASS` — the corrected deadline survived 3 real process restarts and
  the recovered record is not pruned. The before/after traces are from the same
  script and state dir; the only difference is the two fixed source files.

- **Subprocess regression test (committed).** The same OS-process-restart flow is
  committed as a real persisted-SQLite regression test in
  `src/tasks/task-registry.store.test.ts` ("persists the corrected deadline
  across real OS process restarts and survives the next sweep"). It spawns the
  fixture `test/fixtures/task-registry-recovery-restart.ts` three times via
  `node --import tsx` (seed → recover → verify) against one
  `withOpenClawTestState` state dir, then reloads and runs the next maintenance
  sweep in the parent. On the pre-fix source this test fails
  (`expected <expired lost-window deadline> to be greater than <now>`); with the
  fix it passes.

- **Regression tests** in `src/tasks/task-registry.store.test.ts`:
  - a `lost` record with the short lost-window `cleanupAfter` is recovered via
    `markTaskTerminalById({ status: "succeeded", ... })`; the recovered record's
    `cleanupAfter` equals the standard terminal retention from the recovered
    `endedAt` and is greater than the stale lost-window value (fails on the

prs.title: fix: deliver ask_user prompts after yielded continuations
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `ask_user` prompts can appear only in Control UI and leave the originating channel turn blocked when a post-`sessions_yield` requester-settle continuation asks a question.

## User Impact

User impact: channel users receive the question in the originating conversation instead of having to discover and answer it in Control UI.

## Why This Change Was Made

The embedded progress controller converted an absent `onToolResult` callback into a truthy no-op callback. The tool lifecycle then reserved the question prompt for that callback even though it could not deliver anything. Embedded tool construction also omitted the direct channel sender needed after preserving callback absence.

This change preserves callback absence and supplies the originating-channel sender only for runs without a lifecycle delivery callback. Normal runs continue using their existing callback, avoiding duplicate delivery.

Requested by [Ian via WebChat](https://jarvis.tail1050ea.ts.net/chat/main/dashboard/e9d23dff-549b-45b5-9c7a-f6148816c98c).

## Evidence

- Added an exact-path callback-less requester-settle Slack loopback test. The same `notifyToolResult` produced by `createEmbeddedRunProgressController` is passed into the real `prepareEmbeddedAttemptToolBase` composition, which constructs the real `ask_user` tool through `createOpenClawCodingTools` and selects `createChannelQuestionPromptDelivery` only because that callback is absent.
- The proof uses the real Slack plugin/Web API adapter against a credential-free local HTTP server. It verifies the originating account token, channel, and thread; canonical single-select Block Kit buttons; exactly one `chat.postMessage`; one answered-state `chat.update`; a single persisted answer claim; rejection of a duplicate claim; answered status; and successful tool resumption containing `Staging`.
- Regression sensitivity was verified by temporarily restoring the broken progress-controller wrapper: the Slack test failed because no prompt reached the callback-less embedded fallback, then passed again after restoring the branch implementation.
- Added production-composition coverage for a Slack-thread requester-settle run with `sourceReplyDeliveryMode: "message_tool_only"` and deliberately conflicting explicit/fallback route fields.
- Retained the independent Telegram loopback transport proof as cross-channel coverage. It captures the Bot API prompt, answers through the question gateway, persists the reply, and verifies successful resumption without duplicate prompt delivery.
- Ordinary channel runs remain on the embedded lifecycle callback and do not construct a competing fallback.
- Final focused validation on the rebased head: 65 tests passed (63 embedded-attempt composition tests plus the Slack and Telegram loopback proofs).
- `pnpm check:changed` passed formatting, core/core-test/test-root typechecks, lint, dead-export scans, boundary checks, and static guards; `git diff --check` passed.
- No production channel, external credential, or model call is used. The Slack proof deterministically executes the real prepared tool rather than relying on a model stream; the exact changed embedded composition and the real question bridge, Slack plugin, and transport remain in the exercised path.

---
[View the OpenClaw team session](https://jarvis.tail1050ea.ts.net/chat/main/dashboard/e9d23dff-549b-45b5-9c7a-f6148816c98c)

prs.title: fix(plugins): unblock repairs while data migrations are pending
prs.body:
Related: #161921, #166554. Backports [#166588](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166588) to `release/2026.10.3`.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes plugin package repairs being refused by the data migration they need to complete, and recovery getting stuck when the matching official ClawHub release is unavailable.

## User Impact

Verified repair packages can be saved while data migrations remain pending; live runtime application and old-source cleanup stay deferred during repair publication. Explicit plugin-entry removal retains the normal config backup and pending data obligations.

An implicit exact official ClawHub target can use its declared trusted npm alternative at the same version. If no allowed source serves it, verified compatible installed code is retained with a retry warning. Existing version pins, source authority, artifact validation, and integrity/security refusals remain authoritative.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is a semantic backport of main `c9c023fbb12d8bfde61af4a228a9170e4f8b3f9b`, preserving the accepted repair-publication versus activation separation and existing target-bound integrity policy. Stable error formatters and the more precise existing advisory assessment are retained. Plugin behavior remains the **18-file, +505/-77** semantic donor. After integrating merged compatibility #170306, the sole adjacent-import conflict preserves both the trusted-source resolver and the plugin-owned runtime catalog. A two-file CI fixture repair brings the current delta to **20 files, +516/-82**; no dependency, production schema, or new CLI/config option changes.

This carries the approved design in #166588, not the abandoned speculative backup-restorer. Neither reported deletion nor every historical #161921 variant is claimed fixed. Codex compatibility and visible update reasons are already merged in #170306; Doctor #170218 is also merged.

The CI-only roster/lifecycle-assertion repair comes from main [#168926](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168926), `ba60b5ff2fb5ef099f79ca391099587f81f1c795`, with the donor’s existing disabled-heartbeat prerequisite from #165541. Published 10.2 refuses the old fixture’s `agents.list` before applying any candidate. Use the existing explicit keyed roster and retain every readiness/update assertion, timeout, cleanup and failure control. The donor’s unrelated node-host SQLite fixture extensions are not included.

## Evidence

- All five donor suites reproduced **seven distinct expected failures** on unchanged 10.3; all **91 focused tests passed** after the port, including real loopback ClawHub/npm publication and activation/data-preservation controls.
- Affected subsystem: **611 tests passed**, 33 files requested (32 passed, one Windows-only file skipped), 267.88s wall. Five existing native Windows tests skip on macOS. Initial parallel setup failed its namespace guard while E2E declaration outputs were being created; the unchanged selection passed once those writers settled. No guard/timeout/skip changes.
- Full changed-file checks passed (1591.55s wall, including SDK-ownership wait), covering production/test types, formatting, lint, dead exports, import cycles, and architecture guards.
- Original independent P1 review raised one integrity-target finding, **explicitly dispositioned, not reported as clean**: existing `update-installed.ts` and `update-channel.ts` bind the catalog digest to its original spec, not another source/version; the existing `update.test.ts` externalization matrix explicitly excludes the original bare-spec digest from a newly selected exact release. This backport keeps that policy; unchanged exact catalog targets retain their digest, differing exact version pins cannot fall back, and authority/integrity/security controls passed.
- Pre-integration published 10.2 updater × exact candidate C=Q=`3c7c197fc0ce83a597588df77c9eae4aa93ce43f` **passed** the existing isolated base/manual-restart Docker lane (700s; 2031.28s including canonical package preparation). This is not the service-backed CI cell or full release qualification. The old service-backed CI failure was the baseline `agents.list` fixture, before applying the candidate. This corrected head includes its main-derived repair without weakening readiness/update assertions; the exact-head real service-backed update cell passed in [CI run 38327903986](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38327903986).

Single-worker standalone wall times: config CLI 86.83s (26 tests), migration publication 100.18s (37), post-core warning 50.41s (15), real-registry publication 1282.28s (6; compiled-runtime preparation dominates), source authority 15.06s (7). macOS arm64, Node 24.16.0, pnpm 12.5.1. Exact-head CI: the real published-driver update step passed in **567s** (complete job **622s**); [run 38327903986](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38327903986) and its required CI gate passed. The complete local package proof is recorded above.

Post-integration evidence (release base `cc35685b3a71866991cd10dabde1026988e05859`):

- **44 tests across five merge-sensitive suites passed**, 715.95s wall: standalone cohort selection, post-core outcomes, and Doctor availability/real-updater/version-drift repair.
- Fresh independent review of the complete corrected backport returned **scoped-clean through P1**, with the existing source-authority/target-binding contracts supplied as evidence. It is distinct from the original findings/disposition above.
- The unmodified native Linux published-driver lifecycle entrypoint passed **all six cases**, 23.88s wall; success, interruption, timeout, status failures and cleanup failures remain asserted, with no product package installed. Initial nested-Docker setup failures are excluded from coverage; readable public-source permissions resolved the fake installer’s pre-start EACCES.
- Full corrected-candidate checks and real service-backed published-driver CI: full changed-file checks **passed**, 1790.44s wall (production/test types, formatting, lint, dead exports, cycles, boundaries and ratchets); the exact-head real service-backed published-driver update cell and required CI gate **passed** in [run 38327903986](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38327903986). Candidate head: `3693b308ae9d8b80d4f4eb83b91eafae49ea9442`.

## Published-10.2 pending-data compatibility proof

P=`openclaw@2026.10.2`; C=the unmodified Linux x64 package from CI run 38327903986, build commit `266c88e9db24d24b5fadd960dd43f23dabf22f70`. Its source tree `d3e9f9f39d2c2d5281b87fb17307345703b94add` is identical to reviewed head `3693b308ae9d8b80d4f4eb83b91eafae49ea9442`. Archive SHA-256: `34b37c3367c5233001f581b527a2571ad57682c64e8bddbe5db67cdccc06faca`. Q uses the maintained process-group/registry helpers at that head plus a private synthetic fixture. Disposable Linux/amd64 account, Node 24.21.0, no live Gateway/state/ports or real provider credentials.

The fixture starts with a real published-10.2-created state schema, installed npm package 1, legacy listener settings, two saved data identities with original creation times, and an existing released-format pending migration receipt (`requiresStateMigration: true`).

- Published 10.2 repair to package 2 **refused** as expected (exit 1, 19.984s): `Plugin settings are not ready for activation`. Old installation record/source, settings, data bytes and pending receipt were unchanged.
- The real published updater applied the exact candidate **successfully** (exit 0, `status: ok`, 1200.188s including managed settlement). Every recorded upgrade step exited 0; the pinned fixture stayed at package 1, its data/settings/receipt survived. Unpublished official Codex availability produced separate advisory warnings, not a rollback; this is not the reporter's actual seven-plugin state.
- Candidate `plugins install` published verified package 2 **successfully** (21.171s), retained the previous source, and warned `activation is deferred`. The migration receipt stayed pending and settings/data remained intact.
- Candidate `doctor --fix --non-interactive` **passed** (63.124s): both original identities/ages remained, listener settings normalized without losing their value or label, the old data remained recoverable byte-for-byte, and the receipt became `completed`.
- A startup-qualified fixture with the same migration/data behavior then verified successful post-Doctor runtime activation and actual reading of the retained data/settings. Its final Doctor control passed in 44.102s.

### Observed startup limit — not a passing deferral control

An additional before-Doctor restart control intentionally declares startup activation and records entry into full registration before reading the not-yet-migrated file. Package publication still defers live application and retains previous code, but a subsequent Gateway restart **does execute registration** while the migration receipt is pending. Registration fails on the missing migrated file; the plugin stays inactive and the Gateway still serves readiness. After Doctor, that same startup-qualified artifact activates and reads the preserved data/settings correctly.

Redacted observed sequence:

```text
published 10.2 repair: exit 1; previous package/settings/data/receipt unchanged
published 10.2 -> exact candidate: exit 0; status=ok; version=2026.10.3
candidate repair: exit 0; package saved; activation is deferred; receipt=pending
Doctor: exit 0; receipt=completed; original identities/ages/settings retained
startup-qualified pre-Doctor control: registrationMode=full; receipt=pending
plugin register: ENOENT current.json; plugin inactive; Gateway ready
startup-qualified post-Doctor control: plugin active; saved data/settings load correctly
```

Current main `c1579cff145163824e05c217803db0cbf619c0be` also has a startup verifier that quarantines payload-verification failures without consuming pending data obligations; its loader/quarantine owners have no pending-obligation check. This source audit is not a main runtime proof. A zero-registration-before-Doctor guarantee would require a separate main-first follow-up or an explicit owner-policy disposition. Do **not** interpret the passing publication/Doctor/data-loading controls as a passing restart-time deferral control or full release qualification.

Initial fixture failures are excluded, preserved, and not labeled product passes: it incorrectly expected the new config shape while the real updater's Doctor held the whole settings object; it lacked a startup activation declaration; its supplemental registry initially mislabeled package 2.1 as 2.0. Corrections changed only fixture/harness code and replayed the affected tail from retained synthetic data, without repeating the successful published updater or changing the candidate. The premature full-registration observation above remains undispositioned.

prs.title: fix(irc): preserve message spacing and release displaced reconnect sockets
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two IRC channel delivery defects:

1. Long outbound messages lose separator spaces at chunk boundaries. `sendPrivmsg` trimmed each chunk and then sliced the remainder by the trimmed length, so whitespace between chunks (indentation, code blocks, doubled spaces) was silently collapsed in the delivered message.
2. An overlapping reconnect can leave a displaced socket connected under the same nick, and a stale socket's later disconnect can tear down the healthy active connection: the `onDisconnect` handler unconditionally nulled `client` and scheduled a reconnect even when the closing socket was no longer the active one.

## User Impact

User impact: IRC recipients get readable, correctly spaced replies (multi-space runs and indentation preserved across 512-byte chunks), and flaky connections no longer risk a lingering duplicate connection under the bot's nick or a spurious reconnect that interrupts a healthy session.

## Why This Change Was Made

- In `sendPrivmsg`, slice the remainder by the trimmed chunk length so whitespace trimmed off a chunk tail stays in `remaining` as the next chunk's leading space, instead of being dropped by trimming both sides.
- In the monitor, `onDisconnect` now ignores a closing socket whose connection epoch no longer matches the active epoch, and `connect` closes a displaced socket it replaces (and retries when a freshly built connection drops before it activates) so no socket is orphaned and the active client is never nulled by a stale disconnect.
- Guarantee forward progress on whitespace-only chunks: `takeIrcPrivmsgChunk` no longer returns an empty prefix when a leading space is its preferred split point, and the send loop carries whitespace-only chunks forward as the leading space of the next non-empty chunk instead of sending an empty `PRIVMSG` and stalling forever.

## Evidence

- New regression test `terminates on whitespace-only chunks and preserves interior space runs`: with `messageChunkMaxChars: 1`, sending `"a  b"` completes, preserves both interior spaces byte-for-byte, and emits no empty `PRIVMSG` body (this hangs on the previous code by repeatedly sending an empty payload).
- New regression test `preserves interior runs of spaces when chunking long text`: `"aaaa bbbb  cccc dddd"` with a low char cap round-trips byte-for-byte through chunking (this fails on the previous code, which delivered `"aaaa bbbb cccc dddd"`).
- Updated `still prefers a nearby space when splitting long PRIVMSG text` to the corrected, space-preserving output `["alpha beta", " gamma"]`.
- Real-loopback monitor coverage (TCP, not mocks): `reconnects when an established IRC socket closes` drops an established socket, then destroys the replacement connection before it activates (`USER` never answered), and asserts the monitor retries and reaches a third ready connection with lifecycle `["ready", "recovering", "recovering", "ready"]` — exercising both the epoch-guarded stale disconnect and the drop-before-activation retry.
- `extensions/irc` suite: 178 passed / 3 skipped (the only failing file is `runtime-api.test.ts`, an environment subprocess-timeout unrelated to this change).
- `git diff --check`: clean.

## Follow-up on re-review (Revision 7: relay-prefix budget + deterministic recovery test)

ClawSweeper's Revision-7 review confirmed no code findings on the previous head and raised two actionable items, both now fixed on `038c21cb685`:

- **Reserve the server relay prefix in the shared byte budget (P2 / merge-risk).** The whitespace-carry path could build a body that fit the client's own 512-byte line but exceeded the server's relayed-line limit once the `:nick!user@host ` prefix was prepended (e.g. 501 -> 520 bytes for `#general`), so a server could reject or truncate the newly combined chunk. The byte budget now reserves the worst-case relay prefix (`~` + USERLEN 10, HOSTLEN 63), coordinating with the same reservation in #159730. All chunking assertions now measure the **relayed** line (`RELAY_PREFIX + PRIVMSG #general :<body>\r\n`) rather than the outgoing line, which is direct recipient-side relay evidence: every chunking case, the 600-space run, and the mixed-whitespace case keep each relayed line at or under 512 bytes while preserving exact byte-for-byte content.
- **Await recovery after the replacement actually disconnects (P2).** The ready-then-drop monitor test previously resolved on the second `ready` patch, which fired before the fixture's timer destroyed the replacement, so the `connectionCount` assertion ran while the socket was still open. The fixture now drops the replacement through an explicit gate (`dropReadyReplacement()`), the test observes the socket close (`readyReplacementClosed`) and awaits the recovered (third `ready`) connection instead of the second-ready signal, then asserts `connectionCount >= 3` and a `ready -> ... -> ready` lifecycle with `recovering` in between.

Verified locally with node 24.16.0:
- `extensions/irc/src/client.test.ts`: 23/23 pass (all relayed-line assertions at or under 512).
- Full IRC suite: 143 passed / 3 skipped across 16/17 files; the only failure is the pre-existing `runtime-api.test.ts` subprocess timeout (environmental, unrelated).
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`: exit 0; oxlint on the changed files: clean.
- The `monitor.test.ts` database-workers shard cannot run green on this machine because a machine-wide Windows sqlite lock (`EBUSY: resource busy or locked, unlink ...openclaw.sqlite`) breaks cleanup for all monitor tests here, including unmodified ones; the new test's assertions pass before that cleanup error. This is the same environment limitation documented for the monitor evidence in prior rounds.

## Follow-up on re-review (Revision 8: recipient-side relay delivery + displaced-socket observations)

ClawSweeper's Revision-8 review (head `038c21cb685`) found no code findings and raised two evidence items, both now addressed on `905ca46c116`:

- **Recipient-side relay delivery (P1).** The prior relay evidence was a budget assertion over a locally constructed prefix; the fixture did not relay messages and had no receiving IRC client. The test now runs a real relay: the loopback server forwards every bot `PRIVMSG` to a separate receiving IRC client connection, prefixing each line with the sender's `nick!user@host` (worst-case USERLEN/HOSTLEN), and the test reads what that receiving client actually parsed. New `irc client PRIVMSG recipient-side relay` cases (`a` + 600 spaces + `b`, NBSP + 600 spaces, and 900 CJK code points) assert the receiving client reconstructs `bodies.join("") === text` byte-for-byte, that every received wire line is at or under 512 bytes, and that no lone surrogates are emitted.
- **Displaced-socket observations (P1).** The reconnect tests now assert socket-level facts: after a ready replacement is dropped and the monitor recovers, `openSocketCount() === 1` (the displaced sockets were closed; no lingering connection under the same nick) and the active socket `destroyed === false`. The multi-account test additionally observes the stopped account's socket `close` while the sibling account keeps the same live, non-destroyed socket (`betaSocket.destroyed === false`) — displacement closes the old connection without disrupting the active one.

Design note on activation-pending coverage: `ingress.pause()` resolves as soon as the pump returns from `drainOnce`, and the drain starts dispatches without awaiting them, so the `await ingressPause` activation window is effectively immediate on a healthy machine — a replacement always reaches the `ready` patch before any server-side drop can land. The displaced-close (`connect` closing `client !== nextClient`) and drop-before-activation retry branches are defensive against a race the single-flight reconnect timer plus the `onDisconnect` epoch guard already prevent; the reachable equivalents are covered by the socket observations above and the existing `ready -> recovering -> ... -> ready` lifecycle assertions.

Verified locally with node 24.16.0:
- `extensions/irc/src/client.test.ts`: 26/26 pass (23 existing + 3 recipient-side relay).
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`: exit 0; oxlint on the changed files: clean.
- `monitor.test.ts` database-workers shard: the ready-then-drop test passes with the new socket assertions (`openSocketCount() === 1`, active `destroyed === false`). The two DB-dependent reconnect tests intermittently time out on this machine under the known Windows sqlite `EBUSY` lock (machine-wide; also fails unmodified tests) and are unchanged in this revision.

prs.title: fix(feishu): deliver card form submissions to plugin handlers
prs.body:
Related: #43202

## What Problem This Solves

Feishu plugins cannot handle card form submissions through the shared connection: the callback parser drops submitted fields, and structured card buttons never reach registered plugin handlers.

## User Impact

Plugins can receive form inputs and selections with the account, sender, conversation, and original card message ID, without starting a model turn. Existing quick-command routing remains in place. This does not change native outbound card rendering or plugin trust.

## Why This Change Was Made

Preserve the named submitted fields as bounded data and route existing `ocf1` button actions to `api.registerInteractiveHandler` namespaces. For example, `a: "expense-form:save"` reaches the `expense-form` handler with payload `save`.

The adapter checks current account and DM/group access after chat lookup, and rejects a config replacement during authorization. Missing original context, unknown chat types, malformed or oversized submitted fields, and unregistered structured buttons cannot fall through to command/model execution. Plugins still own their card binding and business authorization.

This deliberately addresses plugin callbacks rather than changing the agent-visible command/JSON contract discussed in #43202.

## Evidence

### Checks on the reviewed PR head

PR head: `05bb7d4dc3074ca25c3a7462fc775ddcf42f654e`.

- Feishu extension lane: **105 files, 2,118 tests passed** on Node 24.19.0 / Vitest 5.
- Production and test extension typechecks, targeted oxlint, formatting, import-cycle and unused-export checks, and the selected `check:changed` guards passed. Full-project test suites were not run.
- Official Feishu runtime build passed (16 entry points). Independent review completed; its configuration-revocation finding was fixed and re-reviewed.
- The exact-head custom distribution completed the canonical build and tarball integrity/import-graph checks and loaded Feishu with `origin=bundled`. Its earlier live attempt reached the structured-action log but did not establish plugin delivery. That unsuccessful attempt is not counted as passing evidence, and its root cause remains unestablished.

### Real Feishu interaction results — September 15, 2026

**Runtime scope:** these successful interactions ran on OpenClaw **2026.9.3**, original baseline `1391f7cd2d40ab5bbcf2f5f831d3a64f520e72d7`, with this PR's seven-file callback patch backported as local build `8b5fb55fda1c123dd2a93f2370f1fa137329d787`. This is backport runtime evidence, **not an exact-head runtime pass for `05bb7d4`**. The backport passed 103 Feishu test files / 2,053 tests, source and package-boundary typechecks, targeted lint, and the canonical bundled-plugin build and tarball checks.

The adapter was genuinely bundled in the installed package and used the existing Gateway connection. A temporary plugin registered through `api.registerInteractiveHandler`. All inputs were synthetic; no application business data was written.

Sanitized observations from the actual handler and message readbacks (UTC):

```text
12:42:20.405 callback_received: action=confirm, step=3
  originalMessage=true, originalChat=true, senderMatched=true
  action fields=[value, tag, form_value, name]
  form fields=[body, date, empty, related]
12:45:33.709 original saved submission revalidated:
  body=true, date=true, related=true, empty=true
  rawFieldsUnchanged=true
12:45:35.271 original_message_readback: step=4, sameMessage=true
12:54:22.663 callback_received: action=image, step=5
12:54:23.817 original_message_readback: step=6, sameMessage=true
12:54:27.516 callback_received: action=cancel, step=6
12:54:29.076 original_message_readback: step=7, sameMessage=true
```

- **Form preservation:** the multiline body retained CRLF and two leading spaces on the second line; the date arrived as `2026-09-16 +0800`; both selected values and the exact empty string were preserved. The fixture initially expected LF and a date without a timezone suffix. Only its assertions and date-picker display formatting were corrected; the original saved callback values were not rewritten or resubmitted. The corrected fixture passed nine focused tests, including rejection of missing indentation and an incorrect date.
- **Original-card updates and cancellation:** message PATCH followed by GET confirmed updates to the same original message. The plugin's cancel callback completed, and the saved form content remained intact. The operator confirmed the retained content and image were visible.
- **Image evidence and limitation:** the real image button reached the handler. The fixture initially read the SDK upload result incorrectly (`data.image_key` instead of the returned root `image_key`). One recovery upload obtained and persisted the key, then updated the original card. The operator confirmed image display; a subsequent real image click reused that key. The first upload response was discarded, so its outcome is unknown: this is **not an exactly-once upload claim or an uninterrupted first-attempt image pass**. Message GET exposed a compatibility view, so visual display is supported by operator confirmation rather than an exact image-key match in GET.
- **Existing quick command:** a real `/help` button click reached the existing quick-command route, and the operator confirmed the help response.
- **Model-call observation:** the fixture recorded zero `model_call_started` events during this run. This is limited hook evidence, not an exhaustive trace of every possible model backend.

After testing, the synthetic card was deactivated and read back, the temporary plugin configuration was removed with a checked baseline restore, and the Gateway remained ready. Maintainer acceptance of the public callback contract and validation scope remains a separate decision; this update does not claim that all merge requirements are cleared.

prs.title: fix(exec): report a run with no captured exit code as failed, not completed
prs.body:
Related: #146426

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a command whose supervised process terminates without ever reporting an exit code is recorded as a successful exit-0 completion, so a run that never produced a status surfaces as success instead of a failure.

## User Impact

Runs that end without a captured exit code now report failed, with the reason shown to the user, and automation reading the exec outcome no longer sees a false success for them. Commands that do report a code — including signal and timeout paths — are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildExecExitOutcome` coerced a null exit code to `0` and still treated the record as a normal exit, so a run that never produced a status took the completed branch: `status: "completed"`, `exitCode: 0`, no failure reason, and an `exec.process.completed outcome:completed` diagnostic.

A null code is not evidence of success. `RunExit.exitCode` is nullable by contract. The outcome now takes the existing failure path, which already classifies this shape as `aborted` and renders "Command aborted before exit code was captured" — so the null is preserved rather than replaced by a sentinel.

This covers the three points in the issue's proposed change: (1) a null code is no longer success, (2) the null is preserved in the payload — the failed branch already returns `exitCode: params.exit.exitCode`, and (3) the regression test asserts the null code survives.

Scope note: a process killed by a signal is unaffected. Signal kills arrive as `reason: "signal"` with a null `exitCode`, which never took the completed branch. This fix is specifically the `reason: "exit"` record that never captured a code.

Non-goals: the supervisor's reason vocabulary and the signal/timeout classifications are untouched. No new config, protocol, or persistence surface.

## Evidence

### A real run reaches this record on Linux — no stub anywhere in the chain

The producer is OpenClaw's own service-child relay host. On non-Windows, `createChildAdapter` takes that path whenever the run owns its process tree or `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER` is set (`src/process/supervisor/adapters/child.ts:150-154`), which is the path a non-PTY exec under an installed service is supervised through.

The trigger: an anchor that loses host-side authority while the command is still alive and outlives the graceful-cancel window.

1. exec starts `/bin/bash --noprofile --norc -c 'trap "" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done'` — a command that ignores SIGTERM.
2. The anchor process receives SIGTERM out of band. The host never calls `kill()`, so its `requestedSignal` stays unset.
3. The anchor's own handler runs `requestCleanup("parent-lost")` and signals its process group; the command ignores it.
4. The 5 s `GRACEFUL_CANCEL_TIMEOUT_MS` grace expires with no root result, so `closeAuthority(reason, hardKill=true)` runs `process.kill(0, "SIGKILL")`. The anchor and the command die together, before any `root-result` is sent.
5. The host sees the closing receipt and observes the group's disappearance (`ESRCH`) with no root result, so `finishAuthorityClose` closes authority as `rootResult = { code: null, signal: requestedSignal ?? null }` → `{ code: null, signal: null }`.
6. The supervisor maps that record to `reason: "exit"`, `exitCode: null` — exactly what `buildExecExitOutcome` receives.

Both rows below are real processes: the real supervisor, the real relay host, a real anchor, and the real `runExecProcess` entry point. Nothing is stubbed, mocked, or injected, and the teardown is a real signal to a real process.

| Step | Observed |
|---|---|
| Real supervisor + relay host + SIGTERM-ignoring command | `RunExit { reason: "exit", exitCode: null, exitSignal: null }` |
| Same teardown at `runExecProcess` **before** this change | `status: "completed", exitCode: 0` — 3/3 runs |
| Same teardown at `runExecProcess` **after** this change | `status: "failed", exitCode: null, failureKind: "aborted", reason: "Command aborted before exit code was captured"` — 3/3 runs |

<details>
<summary>Before the change — a run with no captured status reports exit 0</summary>

```text
=== A: real supervisor, real relay host, real process ===
[A]   pid=2067050 argv=/bin/bash --noprofile --norc -c trap "" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done
[A] SIGTERM -> anchor 2067029 at +61ms
[A] waited 5089ms after the signal
[A] RunExit {
  "reason": "exit",
  "exitCode": null,
  "exitSignal": null,
  "oomScoreWrapperSelected": true,
  "durationMs": 5797,
  "stdout": "",
  "stderr": "",
  "timedOut": false,
  "noOutputTimedOut": false
}
=== B: real runExecProcess entry point ===
[B] SIGTERM -> anchor 2068103 at +71ms
[B] waited 5103ms after the signal
[B] ExecProcessOutcome {
  "status": "completed",
  "exitCode": 0,
  "exitSignal": null,
  "exitReason": "exit",
  "durationMs": 7027,
  "aggregated": "",
  "timedOut": false,
  "noOutputTimedOut": false
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>After the change — the same teardown reports failure with the null preserved</summary>

```text
=== A: real supervisor, real relay host, real process ===
[A]   pid=2065282 argv=/bin/bash --noprofile --norc -c trap "" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done
[A] SIGTERM -> anchor 2065267 at +61ms
[A] waited 5090ms after the signal
[A] RunExit {
  "reason": "exit",
  "exitCode": null,
  "exitSignal": null,
  "oomScoreWrapperSelected": true,
  "durationMs": 5736,
  "stdout": "",
  "stderr": "",
  "timedOut": false,
  "noOutputTimedOut": false
}
=== B: real runExecProcess entry point ===
[B] SIGTERM -> anchor 2065793 at +51ms
[B] waited 5081ms after the signal
[B] ExecProcessOutcome {
  "status": "failed",
  "exitCode": null,
  "exitSignal": null,
  "exitReason": "exit",
  "durationMs": 6484,
  "aggregated": "",
  "timedOut": false,
  "noOutputTimedOut": false,
  "failureKind": "aborted",
  "oomScoreWrapperSelected": true,
  "reason": "Command aborted before exit code was captured"
}
```
</details>

Repeated runs of the identical probe are stable in both directions: 3/3 `completed` with `exitCode: 0` before the change, 3/3 `failed` with `exitCode: null` after it.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (scratch probe, run from the repository root; not part of the change)</summary>

```ts
// tmp-probe.mts — real runExecProcess, real supervisor, real anchor
import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { runExecProcess } from "./src/agents/bash-tools.exec-runtime.js";

const PROGRAM = 'trap "" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done';

function ppidOf(pid: number): number {
  try {
    const match = /^PPid:\s+(\d+)$/m.exec(readFileSync(`/proc/${pid}/status`, "utf8"));
    return match ? Number(match[1]) : -1;
  } catch {
    return -1;
  }
}

// Our own anchor only: anchor -> relay -> this probe.
function findAnchorPid(): number | undefined {
  for (const entry of readdirSync("/proc")) {
    if (!/^\d+$/.test(entry)) continue;
    const pid = Number(entry);
    if (pid === process.pid) continue;
    try {
      if (!readFileSync(`/proc/${entry}/cmdline`, "utf8").includes("service-child-group-anchor")) {
        continue;
      }
    } catch {
      continue;
    }
    if (ppidOf(ppidOf(pid)) === process.pid) return pid;
  }
  return undefined;
}

const handle = await runExecProcess({
  // exec runs this as the `-c` program of its own shell, so that shell is the
  // root process and it ignores SIGTERM itself.
  command: PROGRAM,
  workdir: "/tmp",
  env: { PATH: process.env.PATH ?? "" },
  usePty: false,
  warnings: [],
  maxOutput: 100_000,
  pendingMaxOutput: 100_000,
  notifyOnExit: false,
  timeoutSec: null,
});

const deadline = Date.now() + 15_000;
let anchorPid: number | undefined;
while (anchorPid === undefined && Date.now() < deadline) {
  anchorPid = findAnchorPid();
  if (anchorPid === undefined) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 25));
}
if (anchorPid === undefined) throw new Error("anchor process never appeared");
process.kill(anchorPid, "SIGTERM");
console.log(JSON.stringify(await handle.promise, null, 2));
```

```bash
OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER=openclaw pnpm tsx tmp-probe.mts
```
</details>

### Sibling paths through the same entry point

Same real entry point, no signal interference, after the change:

| Command | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `true` | `completed`, `exitCode 0` |
| `exit 3` | `completed`, `exitCode 3` |
| unknown command | `failed`, `exitCode 127`, `shell-command-not-found` |
| `kill -9 $$` | `failed`, `exitCode null`, `exitSignal SIGKILL`, `exitReason signal`, `failureKind signal` |

Only the null-code `"exit"` record changed classification; the signal, not-found, and ordinary exit paths are untouched.

### Regression coverage

| Path | Mode | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| New case in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-foreground-failures.test.ts` | `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/bash-tools.exec-foreground-failures.test.ts` | Before fix: FAIL — 1 failed, 21 passed. After fix: PASS — 22 passed |
| 5 exec suites (`exec-runtime`, `exec-foreground-failures`, `exec-runtime-output`, `exec-runtime.cleanup`, `process.activity`) | `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs <files>` | 80 passed |
| Repo gate | `pnpm check:changed` | pass (`GATE_EXIT=0`; lanes core+coreTests, oxfmt, typecheck, lint, all guards) |

The unit-level case asserts the same record through `runExecProcess` at the seam the existing exec suites use, so the fix stays covered in CI without depending on process signals. Before the fix it failed as `expected { status: 'completed', exitCode: 0 } to match { status: 'failed', exitCode: null }`.

### What was not tested

- No Windows host was available. The relay-host closure above is now reproduced on Linux; the Windows job-object hard-kill path (`useWindowsJobAnchor`) is still unexercised, and it is the likeliest other producer of this record.
- The last settle that can still carry a null code is unreachable by construction, not untested: the PTY adapter's `dispose()` settle is a no-op because the supervisor disposes only after that adapter's `wait()` has already resolved, and `settleWait` ignores a second settlement.
- The reproduction above constructs the trigger deliberately (out-of-band SIGTERM to the anchor plus a command that ignores SIGTERM) rather than waiting for it to happen in the field; it exercises real shipped code, but no production incident was captured.
- No live channel or Gateway proof: the change is local to exec outcome classification.

## Merge conflict resolved and validation refreshed

This revision resolves the merge conflict against `main` that ClawSweeper recorded as the only
remaining item, and re-runs the focused exec validation on the resulting head.

The branch was rebased onto current `main`. The only content conflict was in
`src/agents/bash-tools.exec-foreground-failures.test.ts`, where `main` had in the meantime moved the
suite to a `fullExec()` / `tool.execute()` idiom and dropped the direct `runExecProcess` call this
branch's test used. The conflicted region was therefore taken from `main` and the regression test was
re-expressed in the current idiom with the same assertions — `status: "failed"`, `exitCode: null`,
`failureKind: "aborted"`, `exitReason: "exit"`, and the reason text
`Command aborted before exit code was captured`. `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts` auto-merged
with the classifier change intact. The diff is unchanged in scope: 2 files, +29/-1, matching the
surface recorded in review.

Validation on the rebased head:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `bash-tools.exec-foreground-failures.test.ts` (owner regression file) | 12/12 pass, including the new null-code case |
| `bash-tools.exec-runtime.test.ts` (sibling suite) | 20/20 pass |
| `supervisor.output-activity.real.test.ts` (real supervisor, real child processes) | 2/2 pass — ordinary exits still classify as `completed` |
| `pnpm tsgo:test:src` | pass |
| scoped `oxlint` on both changed files | 0 warnings, 0 errors |

Environment limitation: this rebase and validation run happened on `darwin` (macOS), where the
Linux-only service-child relay host path cannot be re-created, so the real-process before/after
traces above were not re-captured here; what was re-run locally is the focused suite plus the real
supervisor test listed above. No Gateway or channel proof applies, because the change is confined to
local exec outcome classification.

prs.title: fix(gateway): retire node connection when pairing changed before dispatch
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a node's pairing becomes stale server-side (device re-paired, pairing revoked, or recreated), the pre-dispatch authorization fence in the Gateway rejects every request from that connection with a retryable `PAIRING_CHANGED` error — but never retires the connection itself. The node keeps its WebSocket open, presence still reports it as Connected, and a client following the documented auto-retry behavior loops on the same rejected requests forever (39 rejected dispatches in ~24 minutes in the reporter's trace).

## Why This Fix

The same stale-pairing predicate is already treated as terminal elsewhere: the watch-node HTTP runtime closes the session when `isConnectionCurrentPairingState` fails (see `watch-node-http.ts`). The dispatch fence was the only path that answered without reconciling. This change settles the captured pairing lease on the node registry before returning the error, which:

- retires node projections (desktop availability, runner inventory, plugin tools, remote skills, invoke streams, authorized run events),
- flips presence to disconnected and broadcasts it,
- marks the transport-owned client invalidated so the WS dispatch loop closes the socket (4001), handing the connection to the client's documented reconnect lifecycle — where the handshake pairing check fails cleanly instead of looping mid-session.

## User Impact

A re-paired or revoked node no longer shows a permanent fake "Connected" state in the Gateway UI/status. The stale connection is cleaned up on its next dispatch instead of silently wedging, and the node app gets a real disconnect/reconnect cycle with an actionable pairing failure.

## Evidence

- `src/gateway/server-methods.authorization.test.ts`: the stale-pairing rejection test now also asserts `invalidateConnectionForPairingChange` was called with the connection id and reason; fails before the fix, passes after.
- New `server-methods.authorization-node-pairing.test.ts`: a node-role request without a connId is still rejected with `PAIRING_CHANGED` and never touches the registry.
- Validation: gateway-server shard suite green (authorization 21 tests incl. both files), `node-registry.test.ts` 159 passed, `nodes.event.test.ts` 6 passed, `tsgo --noEmit` clean on a fresh install, oxfmt/oxlint clean.

Closes #148693


## Update (ac019f45467) — lease outcomes preserved and live transport proof

**Review finding addressed:** the pre-dispatch fence used `isConnectionCurrentPairingState`, which collapses the registry's three lease outcomes (`current` / `stale` / `unavailable`) into a boolean. That could retire a connection whose pairing store was merely unreadable. The fence now consumes the settled outcome via a new narrow registry method, `resolveConnectionPairingState(connId)`: only a definitively `stale` pairing invalidates the registry session; `unavailable` stays retryable and the connection is preserved, matching the registry's own settlement contracts. `isConnectionCurrentPairingState` delegates to the same method, so existing callers keep their behavior.

**Transport close ordering:** invalidation fences buffered requests synchronously, and the socket is closed (4001) after the rejection frame is written, so the client sees the reason and starts its reconnect lifecycle instead of retrying forever.

**Real behavior proof** (`src/gateway/server.node-pairing-retirement.test.ts`, live Gateway + WebSocket): two paired nodes connect over the real transport, the persisted pairing of one is revoked, and its next dispatch is rejected with `PAIRING_CHANGED`; the obsolete socket closes (`gateway closed (4001): client invalidated: node pairing changed before request dispatch`), the node drops out of `node.list` presence, and the second node keeps its connection and stays listed connected. This runs in CI, so the trace is reproducible rather than a one-off capture.

Validation: node-registry 160/160, authorization + guard + live retirement 23/23, node-pairing authz 43/43 with these files, watch-node-http green, `tsgo --noEmit` clean, oxfmt/oxlint clean.


## Update (7a4290c16d4) — retirement scoped to the rejected connection

Both P1 findings were about the retirement step, and both are fixed by removing the extra invalidation and narrowing the close:

- **Limit retirement to the rejected physical connection:** the fence no longer calls `disconnectClientsForDevice` (which closed every node transport for that device, including an authorized same-device replacement). A new conn-scoped `disconnectClientForConnection(connId)` retires exactly the rejected socket after the rejection frame is written. The replacement keeps its transport and stays dispatchable.
- **Preserve sessions promoted during the pairing lookup:** the fence no longer calls `invalidateConnectionForPairingChange(connId)`, which looked up whatever session currently matched the connection and could retire a generation approved mid-lookup. The captured lease is already settled by `resolveConnectionPairingState` (`invalidateStale: true`), which by design leaves a promoted session intact.

**Proof added** (`server.node-pairing-retirement.test.ts`, live Gateway + WebSocket): a second connection for the same device replaces the first in the registry while the first socket stays open; the obsolete socket's next request is rejected with `PAIRING_CHANGED` and that socket closes (4001), while the replacement stays connected and present in `node.list`. The existing revocation case still passes, and the fence contract test now asserts the conn-scoped close and that no conn-wide invalidation happens.


## Update (6a243d4796d) — promotion survival at the retirement step

Revision 5 kept one P1: the stale-pairing lookup can return `stale` for the captured lease while `node.pair.approve` promotes the same connection through `updateSurface`. The retirement timer then still closed that connection by connId, so a legitimately promoted node lost its transport even though the extra registry invalidation was gone.

The retirement decision is now revalidated at the side effect: the deferred callback re-reads the connection's pairing state and closes only when it still reads `stale`. A session promoted while the first lookup awaited persistence reads `current`, keeps its socket, and the earlier request stays rejected — the capture-time authority still does not authorize that dispatch.

**Proof:** a new contract case pins the interleaving deterministically — first lookup `stale`, revalidation `current` → `disconnectClientForConnection` is never called while the request is still rejected with `PAIRING_CHANGED`; the plain stale case (both `stale`) still closes. The live revocation and same-device replacement cases continue to pass.


## Update (d21c3b44d4b) — retirement decided atomically against the captured lease

Revision 6 kept the same P1: re-reading authority after the await still left a window where a promotion landing during the revalidation was closed with the obsolete lease. The decision now lives in the registry and runs synchronously against a generation captured before the lookup:

- `pairingGenerationForConnection(connId)` captures the live generation at dispatch time.
- `retireRejectedConnection({connId, observedGeneration, reason})` decides atomically — no await between the comparison and the invalidation:
  - a different live generation ⇒ **preserve** (promotion survived, transport stays open),
  - the captured generation still live ⇒ **retire** (stale session invalidated, transport closes),
  - a connection missing from the registry ⇒ **obsolete** (a replacement already retired it; close the leftover socket).

The fence closes the transport only when the outcome is not `preserve`, so the earlier request is still rejected while a promoted node keeps its socket.

**Tests:** registry case pins all three outcomes and that a promoted generation is never invalidated; the fence contract case drives the promotion interleaving through dispatch and asserts `retireRejectedConnection` is called with the captured generation and no transport close; the live revocation and same-device replacement cases continue to pass.


## Update (107b20ad2a0) — strict generation comparison

Revision 7's P1: the retirement comparison skipped the absent case, so a lease captured without a pairing generation could still retire a session that gained one while the lookup awaited persistence. The comparison now requires strict equality, so an absent capture also defers to a promoted session; a session that is still generation-less retires as before.


## Update (75e2bbe54f5) — rebased onto current main, body refreshed

Merged `origin/main` into the branch (no history rewrite, so no force-push): the only conflict was `src/gateway/server-methods.ts`, where main had moved the authorization fence into the prepared-session-mutation flow. The node-pairing retirement now sits inside that flow, keeping main's `details: { code: "PAIRING_CHANGED" }` error shape and the trailing `sessionMutationAuthorization` return. The branch is now 0 commits behind main; the worktree dependencies were reinstalled for the merged lockfile.

One follow-up commit: the retire decision re-reads `node.client.invalidated` after the owner call that sets it, instead of reusing the pre-call value.

Verification after the merge:

- `src/gateway/node-registry.test.ts` + `src/gateway/server.node-pairing-retirement.test.ts` + `src/gateway/server-methods.authorization-node-pairing.test.ts`: 167 passed.
- `tsgo` core: clean; `oxfmt --check`: clean.
- The "Why This Fix" opening above now names the settled-lease mechanism the code actually uses (the earlier `invalidateConnectionForPairingChange` wording was stale).

Still open from the review: production-registry and transport evidence for promotion from absent and existing generations (live verification).

## Update — live transport proof

`server.node-pairing-retirement.test.ts` spawns a real Gateway process, connects two WS node connections with persisted pairing state, and exercises the transport boundary:

```
✓ node pairing retirement over the live transport > retires the stale connection and keeps the valid node dispatchable 286ms
✓ node pairing retirement over the live transport > retires an obsolete socket without closing its same-device replacement 120ms
Test Files  1 passed (1) | Tests  2 passed (2)
```

- **Test 1**: one node's pairing is revoked; its WS transport receives close code 4001 with reason `node pairing changed before request dispatch`; presence drops the stale node while the other valid node stays dispatchable.
- **Test 2**: a same-device replacement has already replaced the old transport; the leftover socket from the obsolete connection is retired without closing the replacement.

This is a real Gateway process (not a mock), real WS connections, and real transport close — CI-runnable, not a one-off screenshot.

prs.title: fix(hooks): preserve Gmail push tokens with reserved characters
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Gmail Pub/Sub callback authentication can fail when the configured push token contains URL-reserved characters.

## User Impact

User impact: user-supplied Gmail push tokens containing characters such as `+`, `/`, `&`, or `=` survive Tailscale endpoint construction without being reinterpreted as query syntax.

## Why This Change Was Made

The push token is an opaque credential value, so the endpoint now percent-encodes it before placing it in the `token` query parameter. The required query-token flow remains unchanged.

## Evidence

The new regression fails 1/32 on the unmodified base because `part+two/&=` is emitted raw. On the rebased candidate:

```text
gmail-setup-utils.test.ts: 32 passed
oxfmt --check: passed
oxlint --deny-warnings: 0 warnings, 0 errors (230 rules)
pnpm tsgo:prod: passed
```

## CI follow-up and remaining proof

Hosted CI remains red on [the voice-call routing job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/34924701889/job/104240339496?pr=148724) and its aggregate gate. Its original routing assertion expected the inbound owner's `createBridge` call once and observed zero. The job tested synthetic merge `a3e8c03b27b315fcf1bc1800b234148d4c6b4872` on Node 24.20.0, with then-main parent `51ea3dbd67e448485d9a13fb4b1839a14fd480e9`, rather than the earlier Node 24.16 PR-head/base replay.

On these frozen merge/main inputs, the complete failing inner group passed on both versions: 15 files / 165 cases each, using the original extension-database-workers owner and max workers 3. This did not reproduce the hosted failure. The bridge-start timestamps are compatible with an asynchronous scheduling hypothesis, but they do not establish the wait-start deadline or the actual `createBridge` call time, and are not a root-cause finding.

The unchanged runner's exact original ordered plan stopped earlier at two memory-write permission fault-injection cases, before reaching voice-call. This explains the additional local fixture sensitivity, not the original GitHub voice-call failure. The nonroot file run is not a complete original-prefix replay.

No production/test source, assertion, timeout, retry or CI guard was changed for this investigation. Original CI cause and preceding execution history remain unresolved; no green hosted CI rerun or absence of indirect effects is claimed. No live Gmail setup or new/existing watcher callback was performed because an authorized account/token was unavailable. These deterministic tests are not live-provider proof.

Live Gmail/Pub/Sub verification remains pending. The available Windows environment has neither gcloud/gog nor an authorized test Gmail account and its OAuth-client GCP project.
