prs.title: feat(cli): add zeroclaw plugin update with verified replacement
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Stacked on #11261, which is stacked on #11236. #11581 has landed on `master` as `ea4a54bb5b`: this branch merged its head first (`0ba2b77343`) and now carries the landed commit through `277aeabb0e`'s merge of `master`. `2f3409e9ba`, `bd2d4e5eea`, `f94508dc69` and `2ec36c26dc` merge #11261's head, now `369fb21334`, which carries #11236's `7a3ad81ed5`. Until they merge, this PR's diff also contains their commits. Please review the eight commits after `0ba2b77343`, up to `bab70cc225`, the follow-ups from `75116ac28a` to `a1d212eca1`, and `f3d0a59844`. `6354484051`, `2f3409e9ba`, `bd2d4e5eea` and `f94508dc69` only merge the base, `2ec36c26dc` with the adaptation described below; `277aeabb0e` and `2b3c93631d` merge `master`, with the resolutions described below.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **The command.** Adds `zeroclaw plugin update`, the missing lifecycle operation from #10995 (#7432 R3, Phase 2 D3). It implements the contract posted on the issue for review: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/10995#issuecomment-5894198515.
    - Syntax: `plugin update <name>[@<version>]...`, `plugin update --all`, and `plugin update <name> --from <dir>`, with `--registry <url>` as for install. Update never installs a package that is not installed.
    - Version selection is install's rule: the last entry the registry lists for a bare name, the exact entry for `name@version`, compared only for equality. An equal version is "up to date" and nothing is downloaded. A different version, even an older one, is installed, so pinning the previous version is the way back. When both are semantic versions and the selected one is older by SemVer precedence, the result line says so (`Replaced 'x' 2.0.0 with 1.2.5, an older version than the one installed.`) instead of reporting an update. A `--from` package always replaces, so a rebuilt plugin can be reinstalled at the same version.
    - Verification is the existing path, reused: the registry download, with its digest when the registry entry lists one, then `PluginHost::admit_update` from the stacked host PR, then the install-time load check with the operator's `plugins.limits`. There is no `--no-verify` for update.
  - **Authority gate.** The runtime grants every permission a manifest requests. So an update is refused, before its component is compiled, when its manifest adds a permission, a capability, or a new `provides` id, or names a different publisher key than the installed version (or none where the installed version named one).
    - The refusal prints the exact command that accepts the difference, with one `--allow-token <item>` per added item, such as `--allow-token permission:<name>`; `--allow` still takes the same items as a comma-separated list. It is pinned to the reviewed version and quoted for the host shell by the egress ceremony's `ShellDialect`, because versions, `provides` ids and keys are publisher-controlled text. Every output line that carries manifest text escapes control, format, line separator and paragraph separator characters (Unicode Cc, Cf, Zl, Zp), line breaks and invisible characters included, so manifest text cannot rewrite, rearrange or disguise the prompt, including an approval block a batch printed earlier, or print a line of its own.
    - `--allow` and `--allow-token` apply to one plugin, and a registry update that uses either must be pinned as `name@version`.
    - The publisher key is a verified identity only under `signature_mode = "strict"`; the docs say so.
  - **Preserved state.** Config rows, secrets, `egress_hosts`, `egress_allow_private`, TLS profiles, durable state, and instance keys are never modified.
    - Missing rows are created without a grant and saved before the package changes, so nothing after the replacement can fail.
    - Egress keeps the never-extend rule: update seeds nothing, even into a row it creates, and prints the same declared-versus-granted difference install prints for an existing row.
    - When preserved config fails the new version's schema, the update still completes and names the instance and the schema location. A missing required property is named, since the name is the schema's own. A configured value, or a configured key the schema does not declare, is never printed, because either could hold a secret.
    - A package whose config row still uses the pre-1.0 package-name key is refused with the same guidance `plugin install` prints (its rename steps, or a deployment-wide egress refusal in their place), one line each under the result; the docs say so.
  - **Results and recovery.** Each plugin gets one result: updated, reinstalled, up to date, skipped (with `--all`, not listed in the registry), needs approval, or not updated with the version kept.
    - A failure does not stop the others, and the command exits 1 when any plugin was not updated.
    - A command that updated anything ends with one restart-the-daemon note, and a batch ends with a summary line.
    - A package an interrupted update displaced is put back by the next `plugin update <name>`, before the registry is consulted, so recovery works offline. Names that are not installed are answered before the registry too, with the install command for the source the update named. `plugin list` and `plugin update --all` point at the recovery with two complete commands (a plugins directory this process cannot lock, such as a read-only one, simply gets no such note in `plugin list`), one from the registry and one from a package directory, rendered for the selected configuration as the approval, install and not-installed commands are, and `--all` never restores a displaced package unasked. An update interrupted mid-swap points back at its own source, so a `--from` run is retried from the same directory; authority the update adds is asked for again.
    - A restored copy the host does not admit is reported with where it now is, and with `plugin list --verbose`, which prints discovery's reason.
  - **Pointers keep the source.** `plugin install` on an installed package now fails with the update command for the same source: `--from <dir>` after a local install, `name@version` after a pinned one. Likewise, `plugin update <name> --from <dir>` for a name that is not installed points at installing that directory. Neither ever offers the registry for a local build, and exit statuses are unchanged.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No new registry, installer, config key, or on-disk format.
  - No version ordering for selection. Semantic versions are compared only to report an older one.
  - No daemon signalling: channel instances keep their component until restart, and tool sets built afterwards load the new version.
  - Channel-instance config and grant seeding stays with #10996. Install's own `<already-installed>` semantics stay with #10162; this PR only adds the pointer.
  - Registry-side compatibility metadata (#9624) does not exist yet; the load check is the compatibility gate.
  - Known limits, documented where operators read them:
    - no `fsync` around the renames, as for install
    - a tool set built at the instant of the swap can be inconsistent once
  - A process killed between publishing the replacement and marking the replaced version for deletion leaves that version claimed in its hidden transaction. Recovery deletes it while the plugin is installed; after a later `plugin remove`, `plugin list` shows it as displaced until a named `plugin update` restores it, and `--all` never does. `plugin remove` leaving such a claim alone is a follow-up.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw plugin install`/`list`/`update`, the root plugin CLI, and five runtime Fluent catalogues.
  - `seed_plugin_config_entries` is split. Its row-finding first half becomes `ensure_plugin_config_entries`, shared with update, and install's behavior and output are unchanged.
  - A batch fetches the registry index once and compares versions before downloading, through `download_registry_entry` from #11581, which this branch merges. This PR no longer defines that function itself.
  - In `zeroclaw-plugins`, `validate_config_instance` names a missing required property in its `InvalidConfig` message, so every surface that reports that error, such as a daemon load failure, names it too. ### What this does, simply

Until now the only way to move a plugin to a new version was to remove it and install the new one, with nothing checking the new version first or keeping the old one working if something went wrong. `zeroclaw plugin update` does it in one step.

It fetches the new version and runs every check a fresh install runs, including that the component actually loads on this host. Only then does it swap the package in. If anything fails before the swap, the old version is untouched; if the swap itself fails, the old version is put back. If the process dies mid-swap, the next update puts the old version back, even without network access.

A plugin's settings, secrets, network grants and stored data are keyed by its name, not its version, so they carry over. If a new version asks for more than the old one had (a new permission, a new capability, or a different publisher key), update stops and prints the exact command that accepts that difference. So an update can never quietly give a plugin more power. Update also never widens a plugin's network allowlist; it prints the command instead.

No new scope. `plugin update` writes only through the host's staged replacement inside the plugins directory, config rows through the existing dirty-path save, and the registry index cache under `data_dir`, as `plugin install` and `plugin search` already do.
- New external network calls? No new destinations: update fetches the registry index and archive the operator selects, exactly as install does.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No. Config rows and secrets are preserved untouched. The config-rejection report prints instance keys, schema locations, and a missing required property's name from the schema. It never prints configured values or undeclared configured keys: unit tests assert a configured value does not appear, and the existing secret-exposure test is unchanged and passes.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes. An update replaces a plugin's bundled skill files, which the model reads.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Adding the `skill` capability is added authority, so it needs `--allow`. Changing skill content under an existing `skill` capability does not, as when the plugin is removed and installed again: the content comes from the package the operator chose, passes the configured signature policy, and passes the staged skill-bundle check discovery applies. The trust-relevant risks of an update, and how each is handled:
  - **Widening a plugin's authority without consent.** Every added permission, capability or `provides` id, and every change of the declared publisher key, is refused unless named in `--allow` for that one pinned plugin. This is decided before the component is compiled. The publisher key is a verified identity only under `strict` signature policy, and the docs state that.
  - **Widening network reach.** Update never seeds or extends `egress_hosts`, even in a row it creates.
  - **A local build replaced by a registry package of the same name.** Update does not record where a package came from, so `plugin update <name>` without `--from`, and `--all`, look the name up in the registry. Under a non-strict signature policy, a registry package of that name that requests no added authority replaces an unsigned local build without approval, because gaining a publisher key is not an increase, and it inherits the instance's config rows, secrets and grants. Strict policy admits no unsigned build in the first place. The docs tell operators with local builds to name plugins explicitly and to add `--from` when recovering one. Pointers printed during a run with a local source keep that source: the install pointer, the approval command and the interrupted-update pointer use `--from <dir>`, and the not-installed pointer installs the directory. The displaced-package note from `plugin list` and `--all` cannot know the source, so it prints two complete commands: one that updates from the registry, and one with `--from <dir>` that updates from a package directory instead. The two never share a command line, because `plugin update` refuses `--from` together with `--registry`.
  - **Losing a working plugin.** Every check precedes the swap, a failed swap restores the previous package, and an interrupted swap is recovered by the next update, offline included.
  - **Shell injection through the printed command.** Versions, `provides` ids and keys come from the manifest, so every value is quoted with the egress ceremony's `ShellDialect`, and a line that no Windows form can pass literally is the marked PowerShell form.
  - **Terminal control sequences at the prompt.** Every output line that carries manifest text escapes control, format, line separator and paragraph separator characters, line breaks and invisible characters included, so manifest text cannot rewrite or rearrange what the operator reads before accepting, or print a line of its own. A value that needed escaping cannot be accepted by pasting the printed command, so it fails closed; removing and reinstalling remains the way to accept it.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Existing commands behave as before, except that `plugin install` on an installed package names the `plugin update` command for the same source in its error. It still fails with the same exit status, and the original error remains in the chain.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: new `zeroclaw plugin update` subcommand and new localized messages.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: none. The subcommand is new, and no existing flag or config changes.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`. No config key, on-disk format, or persisted state is introduced. Config rows an update created are ordinary empty `[[plugins.entries]]` rows, like the ones install creates.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:**
  - `zeroclaw plugin update` reporting an update while `plugin info <name>` shows the old version.
  - A plugin missing from `plugin list` together with a `Note: an interrupted update left ...` line.
  - A hidden `.<name>.replacing-v1-<id>` directory holding a package that `plugin update <name>` does not put back.

prs.title: fix(rpc): refuse persisted log reads to scoped principals
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `logs/query` and `logs/get` now run `require_global_stream_access` before anything else, the check `logs/subscribe`, `events/subscribe`, and `events/history` already run. Both were gated only by the coarse `Logs:Read` grant, so a scoped principal holding it could read every persisted log record.
  - Those records include authorization-denial audit records, which name agents, config paths, and cron jobs. Sharpest case: `cron/get` on another agent's job deliberately answers "Cron job not found" so the guard is not an existence oracle, yet the caller could then read its own denial record (`Principal is not entitled to agent "beta", which owns cron job "…"`) through `logs/query`.
  - The check resolves the principal against its current grants (`current_authority`), so a demoted administrator is refused on its next request, not at reconnect. The refusal is `FORBIDDEN` and audited like the streams' refusals.
  - The refusal message and the predicate's doc now name the persisted log. The `open_subscription` doc paragraph that had drifted onto `require_global_stream_access` moves back to its function.
  - Docs: `security/authentication.md` lists the five daemon-wide log and event reads as administrator and shared-operator only, and extends the subscription-recheck bullet to `events/subscribe` and to losing administrator rights; `architecture/logging.md`'s Authority bullet now covers `logs/query` and `logs/get`.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to who may use the streams or `events/history` (only their refusal message changes, with the shared text), the `Method::authz` classification (`Logs:Read` is still required), the gateway's `/api/logs` (pairing-only, so it already serves only the shared operator), log persistence, or the fields denial records carry. No per-principal filtering of the persisted log: records do not carry reliable ownership.
- **Blast radius:** RPC clients reading the persisted log as a scoped principal (authenticated roster or OIDC principal without `admin`) now get `FORBIDDEN`. zerocode never reaches `logs/query` or `logs/get` for a principal that is scoped when it connects: its Logs pane opens `logs/subscribe` first, and that method already refuses it. A zerocode session whose principal is demoted while connected already lost its live stream at the next delivery; now its Logs pane also gets `FORBIDDEN` when paging history, which it treats as the end of history; applying or clearing a run filter leaves the pane empty; and its detail view falls back to the event data the row already holds. Administrators, the shared operator, and the web dashboard are unaffected.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11289. This PR lands before #11289; #11330 has already merged. #11289 already updates the denial documentation, the `global_stream_scoped` reason row, and the `rpc-auth-global-stream-scoped` string for these persisted-log refusals. It deletes `GLOBAL_STREAM_SCOPED_DENIAL`, whose text this PR edits; when rebasing #11289 after this lands, retain that deletion in the modify/delete conflict.

### What this does, simply

Several people can connect to one ZeroClaw daemon over RPC, each with their own permissions. A "scoped" user is any signed-in user who is not an administrator: they see only their own sessions, even when allowed to use every agent. The daemon's log mixes everyone's activity, including records of requests the daemon refused and why. The live log and event streams were already closed to scoped users for that reason, but the two methods that read the saved log were not: anyone allowed to read logs at all could read the whole saved log, including details the daemon had deliberately kept from them. This PR gives those two methods the streams' rule: only administrators and the shared operator (the daemon's own account, or a client holding a gateway pairing token) may read the saved log. Everything else about logging is unchanged.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, as an A/B with the dispatcher tests; a manual repro needs a multi-user roster and peer-uid sockets.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** RPC `logs/query` and `logs/get`, consumed by zerocode's Logs pane (`surface` `tui`).
- **Setup / preconditions:** None beyond the Rust toolchain.
- **Steps to run:** `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads`, then delete the two added `self.require_global_stream_access(Method::Logs…)?;` lines in `handle_logs_query` and `handle_logs_get` and rerun.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Both tests pass.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Both fail, and the assertion prints the leaked record: right after `cron/get` told scoped `alice` (agent `alpha`, `Logs:Read`) that the `beta` job was not found, her `logs/query` returns the record naming `beta` and the job.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The Rust lint and test jobs (including the parallel runtime test gate) cover the dispatcher change; the docs style and links jobs cover the two Markdown files.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None for this change. Two runtime tests fail locally for reasons outside this diff: `new_session_methods_are_denied_without_their_grants` fails on macOS even when run alone, at the `session/steer` workspace check on a `/var/folders` temp path (a fixture bug; #11630 fixes it), and `peer_turn_cost_scope_through_execute_boundary_attributes_recipient_and_shares_budget` failed in every full parallel run on both `master` and this branch (#11350 fixes it).
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
# head 1b7bc6351d = 7d461fa56b + merge of master 3500014d92 (9f556f18fd) + the audit-record test
# mutation 1: delete the two handler checks; both tests fail and print the leaked record
#   (same result as the original red run against the unfixed handlers on f151c2e00d)
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_refuse_a_scoped_principal ... FAILED
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_serve_unscoped_principals_until_demoted ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed: uid 4242 logs/query: {"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"at_end":true,"events":[{... "code":-32602,"method":"cron/get","principal_id":"user:alice","reason":"Principal is not entitled to agent \"beta\", which owns cron job \"06f1c291-…\""} ...
  left: Null
 right: Number(-32012)

# mutation 2: delete the audit_denial call in require_global_stream_access;
#   every refusal still holds, and only the new audit-record check fails
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_serve_unscoped_principals_until_demoted ... ok
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_refuse_a_scoped_principal ... FAILED
user:alice's refused logs/query must leave a denial record: {"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"at_end":true,"events":[] ...

# restored: cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- rpc::
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_refuse_a_scoped_principal ... ok
test rpc::dispatch::tests::persisted_log_reads_serve_unscoped_principals_until_demoted ... ok
test result: FAILED. 841 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 4881 filtered out
# the failure is new_session_methods_are_denied_without_their_grants (see the coverage-gap note)

# cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: FAILED. 5713 passed; 2 failed; 8 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
# new_session_methods_are_denied_without_their_grants and
#   peer_turn_cost_scope_through_execute_boundary_attributes_recipient_and_shares_budget

cargo fmt -p zeroclaw-runtime -- --check                         # clean
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings    # clean
scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh       # No prose em-dashes; markdownlint Summary: 0 error(s)
scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh         # No added links detected in changed docs lines.
python3 scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.py <list naming dispatch.rs>   # Comment hygiene gate passed.
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The tests send real requests through `process_line` (the authorization gate, then the handler) against a real `rolling` JSONL writer, and the record at stake is a real denial that `cron/get`'s entitlement guard wrote. Covered: a principal scoped to one agent and one holding `*` are both refused on both methods, with no record content in the response; an administrator and the shared operator read the record through both methods; demoting the administrator (it keeps `Logs:Read` and gains `*`) refuses its next read on the same connection; after the scoped refusals, the administrator reads back one `FORBIDDEN` denial record per refused principal and method. Not verified: a live daemon with zerocode connected; the zerocode behavior described under Blast radius, including a demoted session's paging, comes from reading the Logs pane's code.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A; no rendering code changed, and a demoted session's refusals take the Logs pane's existing error paths.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** 1b7bc6351d (7d461fa56b plus a merge of master 3500014d92 and the audit-record test) on macOS arm64; RPC dispatcher tests in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Workspace-wide `cargo test` and `cargo clippy`: the change is confined to two private handlers in `zeroclaw-runtime`, with no public API change. `scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh` could not run locally because this machine's `rg` is missing its pcre2 library, so its Python checker ran on `dispatch.rs` directly.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No; this narrows access.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A. The PR closes a disclosure: scoped principals holding `Logs:Read` could read other principals' activity and the audit records of refusals, including details a refusal deliberately withheld from its client.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, by design: authenticated non-admin principals that read the persisted log through `logs/query` or `logs/get` are now refused. Reviewers classified this as a security fix rather than a breaking change (those reads should never have been served), so the title carries no `!`.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: a principal that must read the persisted log needs a permission profile with `admin = true`, or must connect as the shared operator. There is no per-principal filtered view.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the squash commit this PR lands as on `master`.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A scoped principal's `logs/query` or `logs/get` returns `-32012` with "Scoped principals cannot read the daemon-wide logs and events…", and the log gains an `RPC authorization denied` record whose `method` is `logs/query` or `logs/get`. A zerocode session whose principal was demoted while connected stops loading older history in its Logs pane, and applying or clearing a run filter leaves that pane empty.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A

prs.title: fix(runtime): reject tool-call envelopes leaked into prose instead of rendering them
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (head `87432f7ae2`; merges cleanly with current master `0f8fb9d372`)
- **What changed and why:**
  - **Symptom.** On `gpt-5.6` via the codex provider (intermittent, about three occurrences in one evening on a production instance), a turn's tool calls arrived glued **into** the visible reply as raw JSON instead of the structured channel: prose, then `{"content":null,"tool_calls":[…]}` followed by a Gemini-style `{"content":…,"tool_code":…,"tool_name":…}` stub, then more prose and a hallucinated success claim. The user saw envelope bytes as garbage text, the tool never executed, and the model then claimed the work was done.
  - **Why every existing layer missed it.** The response starts with prose, so the whole-response JSON pass and every envelope classifier — all gated on the text *starting* with `{`/`[`/tag/fence — never fire. The field payload was additionally malformed by a python-style `\'` escape inside the `arguments` string: invalid JSON, plausibly why the provider delivered the calls as text in the first place.
  - **Fix: detect and retry, never execute.** A complete tool protocol object naming an active tool — after prose, inside other JSON, or inside malformed outer text — now trips the parse-issue path in `detect_tool_call_parse_issue_for_known_tools`, so the turn is rejected and retried with model feedback instead of rendered. Detection scans for JSON values, walks each parsed value's whole tree, and covers canonical, alias- and Responses-shaped envelopes, malformed protocol members of a complete envelope, and python tool stubs. A `\'`-repaired copy is scanned (removed only at odd backslash-run parity, so the legal `\\'` is untouched), so the observed malformed payload is still seen. Every leak-detection site that decides whether a name in model output refers to an active tool applies the parser's alias normalization, so a leak naming `bash` is treated like one naming `shell`. The detector is deliberately bounded to these shapes; what it does not cover is listed under Security.
  - **Why not execute the leaked call.** An earlier revision of this PR salvaged calls from prose. Review showed, and three further review passes on progressively stricter scanners confirmed, that whether an embedded object is a genuine leak or data the model is quoting (a JSON array, a truncated transcript tail, a YAML-style mapping) cannot be decided from text. Executing it therefore lets model-echoed business data smuggle a tool invocation. Rejection with retry fixes the user-visible defect — no protocol bytes rendered, no false completion — while the model re-issues the call through the structured channel.
  - **Streaming parity.** Final rejection cannot retract text already streamed, so the stream guard reaches the completed-response verdict from the same inputs. It holds an unfinished JSON-like value from its own opener, so a leak split across deltas is not forwarded before an identifying key arrives, while ordinary inline JSON in prose keeps streaming; brackets inside strings do not count, and the per-chunk scan is bounded by bytes examined so a run of closed values cannot crowd out a later unfinished candidate. It receives the active tool names from the turn's own tool specs, independently of whether the provider request carries native tool specs, so the text-tool route is covered. It checks the whole buffer on every release, because a release emits everything ahead of the candidate anchor too.
  - **Documentation guard.** A reply that quotes the protocol while explaining it is not rejected, on the completed and the streaming path. Two questions are answered separately. `looks_like_tool_protocol_example` decides whether the reply is documentation; for tag- and fence-delimited calls that is judged for the reply as a whole by any example or sample wording in its visible text ("Sample tool call:", "Example tool call:", "示例如下:", or an explicit framing phrase), because tags are an executable format and a tag that is not documentation is parsed as a real call. `unframed_embedded_protocol_mentions_known_tool` then rejects a reply that is documentation as a whole but carries a bare protocol object naming an active tool without its own framing clause, so one illustrated example exempts only itself. Framing is explicit illustrative phrasing in the clause that ends at the object: only prose counts, so quoted data cannot frame the leak after it; a sentence terminator or a line break closes the clause, with a fence opener excepted and the periods of "e.g." not counted; and a stray tag marker without its own closer is not a span that can hide a leak. Ordinary narration words ("creating the sample page", `examples/`, documentation-domain links) never qualify.
- **Scope boundary:** No text-embedded envelope is ever parsed into a call. No change to the structured tool-call channel, to any provider's request/response mapping, to the whole-response parse passes, to retry policy, or to tool approval. Only the observed `\'` defect is repaired; other malformations are not. The provider-side root cause is not addressed.
- **Blast radius:** The runtime's known-tool parse-issue detection (every provider's text path), the streaming protocol hold-back, and the channel orchestrator's stripping of isolated tool-call artifacts, which now recognizes aliased tool names as its envelope branch already did. A false positive rejects and retries a reply that quotes a complete protocol object naming an active tool without framing it (see Security). A shape outside the detector's scope is rendered as text.
- **Linked issue(s):** No tracking issue was filed; the defect was diagnosed directly from production payloads. Related #10445 (landed; this branch was rebased onto it at the reviewer's request).
- **Labels:** `bug`, `agent`, `channel`, `runtime`, `experienced contributor`, `channel:core`, `domain:security`, `risk:high`, `size:XL`, `topic:provider-transport`

### What this does, simply

Sometimes a model answers in words but also pastes a tool call into the text, as raw JSON, instead of sending it through the proper channel. Before this change, that pasted text was shown to the user as if it were part of the answer, and in one version of this fix it was even run. Now the runtime notices a complete tool call hiding in the text, refuses the whole reply, and asks the model again, so the user never sees protocol bytes and nothing pasted into prose is ever executed. The streaming path holds back the same text before it reaches the screen, since a rejection cannot take back what was already shown. A reply that merely explains or quotes the format as an example ("for example, a call looks like this: …", in English, Spanish, French, Japanese or Chinese) is left alone.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — the leak is intermittent and provider-side, so a live A/B cannot be reproduced on demand; the byte-exact field payloads are replayed deterministically in the regression suite instead.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required workspace build/clippy/test matrix covers the three changed crates; the change is Rust-only with no visual surface. At head `87432f7ae2` (run 38075876268) the [CI Required Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114284927332) passes, with [Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600299), [Lint](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600273) including the rustdoc gate, [Security](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600005) and [Parallel Runtime Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282696530) green; 48 jobs succeeded and none failed.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None for the detection boundary — every placement and guard rule is pinned by a deterministic regression. Documented detection gaps are listed under Security.
- **Commands run and tail output (at head `87432f7ae2`; exit codes captured from cargo itself):**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                        # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings   # clean
$ RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels   # clean
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: ok. 224 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored      (zeroclaw-tool-call-parser)
test result: ok. 5644 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored     (zeroclaw-runtime)
$ bash scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh    # defaults, 3 runs x 16 threads: runtime 5644 and channels 1972 on every run
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh          # passed
```
The same gates pass on the merge result with current `master` (`0f8fb9d372`).

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Both byte-exact field payloads are detected and produce no call; the first is left untouched as visible text for the runtime to reject. At the stream boundary: a python-stub leak split at every byte boundary is never forwarded; the text-tool route suppresses it with no native tool specs; an example framed in an earlier delta streams unchanged, and a framed stub split at every byte still streams whole, while an unrelated earlier phrase exempts nothing; a framed illustration followed by an unframed leak, in one delta or several, suppresses the leak, as does a tag example followed by a bare leak; a unicode-escaped key or a named tool-result envelope ahead of the candidate anchor is not released; and inline JSON in prose keeps streaming. Parser regressions cover every placement surfaced across the reviews — the reviewer's prose-prefixed business array, array-wrapped leaks, complete envelopes inside valid, truncated or malformed outer arrays and objects, closers hidden in double- and single-quoted strings, apostrophes and inch marks, repaired `\'` escapes, tag-adjacent and `<think>`-wrapped structure, a quoted transcript tail, a tuple, and plain narration — each asserting no call, detection, and that the documentation guard stays off; alias names on the stub, tag and malformed-text arms; quoted data that tries to frame a following leak; a line break closing the framing clause; "e.g." framing only its own clause, while "i.e." and a snake_case `page_g_2` frame nothing; stray and plural tag markers that must not hide a leak; a tag or fenced example beside a separate unframed leak; and genuine documentation, including a second framed example, that stays exempt. At the runtime boundary: leaked envelopes and stubs are rejected with no tool call; a tag example beside a bare leak is rejected without its tag executing; five ordinary tag-documentation replies (period-ended lead-in, a dotted file name, a transcript, a numbered list, a trailing explanation after a fence) render with no call; and five ordinary replies (an API explanation quoting a tool result, a Python code sample, an elided example, markdown-link prose, a framed envelope) render without a retry. Every mechanism was mutation-checked: reverting it fails a dedicated regression. Two named exceptions: the stream guard applies the unframed check at both the candidate and the release site, and each alone is backstopped by the other, so only removing both fails the streaming regression; and the candidate-level framing check is backstopped by the whole-buffer release check. NOT verified: a live provider reproduction (intermittent).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no interface presentation changed; leaked protocol bytes are no longer rendered.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `87432f7ae2`; no interface surface. Evidence is the exact-head CI above and the deterministic stream-guard, parser and runtime-boundary regressions.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** A reply embedding an unframed complete protocol object for an active tool is suppressed from the stream and rejected for retry; a reply that frames it as an explicit example is streamed and rendered unchanged, and a documented tag call is rendered, not executed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full-workspace clippy/test left to CI; the scoped runs and CI's parallel runtime gate above cover the three changed crates.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No — fixtures reproduce the leak's structure with illustrative command strings and no personal data.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes**
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: this changes how untrusted model output that embeds tool protocol JSON is handled — it is rejected and retried instead of rendered. Nothing embedded in text is ever executed, so model-echoed data cannot trigger a tool. Residual risks: (1) a reply that quotes a complete protocol object naming an active tool without an explicit example phrase in its own clause is rejected, and if the model keeps quoting it the retries end in the existing fallback error; (2) the detector is bounded, and these are not detected, so such replies are rendered as text: an object that is itself cut off and never closes, replies longer than the 64 KiB scan bound, a tool result that names no tool, a bare call object with no container key (the channel orchestrator strips it only when it stands alone on a line outside a code fence), a duplicate or whitespace-padded protocol key, and a tag leak in a reply whose visible text uses example or sample wording, which is rendered as text rather than executed.

- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

prs.title: fix(mcp): relocate tool-result images to a user message (OpenAI-compatible 400)
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** #10448 added `tool_result_image_policy` with two modes — `image_url` (keep the image as an `image_url` part **inside the `role:"tool"` message**) and `omit` (drop the image, leave a notice). On OpenAI-compatible endpoints that reject image parts in a tool result (HTTP 400 — reproduced on opencode zen / mimo-v2.5; llama.cpp behaves the same), the `image_url` default still 400s, and `omit` avoids the 400 only by **discarding the image** so the model never sees it. There was no mode that both avoids the 400 **and** delivers the image. This PR adds a third mode, **`relocate`**, and makes it the **default**: after native-message conversion, each `image_url` part is moved out of its `role:"tool"` message into a following `role:"user"` message (merged into an adjacent user message when one is present); the tool message keeps its text. Each relocated image group is prefixed with a **bounded local ordinal** label (`[external tool output - image from tool result N]`). The producing tool message carries the same ordinal in a relocation marker, so image-to-call attribution survives the move — bare image bytes alone would let the model attribute an observation to the wrong tool across a parallel batch. The provider-returned (or reconstructed) `tool_call_id` is deliberately **not** echoed into this user-role text; the real id stays on the `role:"tool"` message for native pairing. The image reaches the model as a native image part — the same shape a bare user-message image request uses — without violating the tool-result schema, so an image-returning MCP tool works out of the box with no per-provider config.
- **Why default (not opt-in):** leaving `image_url` as the default means every image-returning MCP tool 400s on the most common OpenAI-compatible endpoints until the user discovers and sets a policy — unnecessary friction. `relocate` uses the user-message image shape supported by the affected endpoints. Providers that never receive image parts (system-merge families, `allow_user_image_parts = false`) are a no-op. This non-lossy path becomes the default; `image_url` and `omit` remain available for explicit opt-in.
- **Bounded label, not the tool_call_id (review fix):** an earlier revision prefixed each relocated group with `[image from tool_call_id <id>]`. The provider-returned id is untrusted, unconstrained text and a reconstruction fallback can even borrow a guessed id, so echoing it into a `role:"user"` message let an instruction-shaped id become model-visible free text and could assert a false producing-call. The label is now a bounded local ordinal computed at relocation; per-call attribution is preserved by stamping the same local ordinal into the producing tool result and its relocated image group, including mixed text-only/image batches. The label identifies the image as external tool output; it is not a guarantee against visual prompt injection. Nothing downstream parses the label back — native tool-call pairing uses the untouched `role:"tool"` `tool_call_id`.
- **Scope boundary:** `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs` (new `ToolResultImagePolicy::Relocate` variant, now `#[default]`, + docs), `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/compatible.rs` (the relocation post-pass, gated on the variant), the provider docs (`configuration.md`, `custom.md`), and the default-coupled test assertion in `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/lib.rs`. The relocation runs under the `relocate` policy; `image_url` and `omit` are byte-for-byte unchanged when selected. Histories with no image-bearing tool message take a fast path and are left untouched. Parallel tool-call batches flush relocated images only once the run of tool messages ends, so a relocated user message never splits a tool result from its siblings. Only native OpenAI-compatible chat-completions providers are affected — direct user images and OpenAI Responses providers are untouched. No API or CLI surface change.
- **Blast radius:** OpenAI-compatible provider request assembly, only for turns where a tool result carries an image. With the new default, such turns now place the image in a following user message instead of inside the tool result — which is what makes them succeed on endpoints that previously 400'd. Turns with no image-bearing tool result, `omit` configs, and explicit `image_url` configs are unchanged.
- **Relationship to #10448:** builds directly on it — same config knob, same conversion surface — and fills the gap its two modes leave (`image_url` → 400 on strict endpoints; `omit` → image discarded). `relocate` is the non-lossy option, and making it the default fixes the 400 for image-returning MCP tools without requiring any configuration. `image_url` (the previous default) stays available for endpoints that accept in-tool images.
- **Refreshed onto current master.** Re-applied on top of master after the approvals: added the `thinking_blocks: None` field that landed with the native-message change, and moved all relocate fixtures from inline `[IMAGE:...]` markers in the result text to the declared `attachments` array, the only source of tool-result images master reads — without that switch the tests would no longer exercise relocation at all. The doc conflicts were resolved on top of master's attachments wording, keeping its statement that legacy tool results pass through unchanged. Added one conversion test that leaves `tool_result_image_policy` untouched, so the default itself is covered rather than only the explicitly-set policy.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #10501.

### What this does, simply

Some OpenAI-compatible servers refuse a request when an image sits inside a tool
result, and answer 400. Until now the only choices were to fail that way or to
throw the image away. This moves the image one message down, into a normal user
message the same servers accept, so the model actually sees what the tool
returned — with no setting to discover first.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — deterministic message-assembly transform, covered by the `compatible.rs` conversion tests.
- **A/B (before → after):** Call an MCP tool that returns an image on a custom OpenAI-compatible provider. **Before (`image_url`, the old default):** the request carries an `image_url` part inside the `role:"tool"` message and the endpoint returns 400. **With `omit`:** no 400, but the model receives only a notice, not the image. **After (`relocate`, the new default):** the image is moved to a `role:"user"` message and the turn succeeds with the image visible to the model — no config needed.

### How I tested

Author-reported local validation on the earlier revision: `cargo test -p zeroclaw-providers --lib compatible::tests::convert_messages_for_native` passed, and `rustfmt --check` was clean.

On c3948b5a927f7b8a6ef2b7d46cc27c847c60c050, the [hosted Test job](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36081372054/job/107903858225) passed and explicitly reports PASS for the policy round-trip and all seven relocate/merge conversion tests, including the two repair regressions below. This checks the production message conversion and serialized image framing; no live provider request was run for this repair.

Conversion tests:

- `convert_messages_for_native_relocates_tool_result_image_to_user_message` — image moves out of the tool message into a following user message labeled `[external tool output - image from tool result 1]`; the tool message keeps its text and real `tool_call_id`, and gains the matching relocation marker.
- `convert_messages_for_native_merges_tool_image_into_following_user_message` — the image merges into an adjacent user message rather than emitting two consecutive `role:"user"` messages.
- `convert_messages_for_native_relocate_labels_each_parallel_call_group` — an assistant message issuing two calls with uneven image counts (call A one image, call B two) keeps the two groups distinct and contiguous, labeled `[external tool output - image from tool result 1]` / `[external tool output - image from tool result 2]`.
- `convert_messages_for_native_relocate_does_not_echo_tool_call_id_into_user_text` (new) — an instruction-shaped id with brackets/whitespace never appears in the relocated user text (the label is the bounded ordinal only).
- `convert_messages_for_native_relocate_labels_missing_id_groups_by_distinct_ordinal` (new) — two id-less groups (the fallback would otherwise borrow the first assistant id) get distinct ordinals, not a borrowed/guessed id.

- `convert_messages_for_native_relocate_links_image_to_its_producing_call_across_identical_text` — moving the sole image between two same-caption calls changes which source tool result carries the matching marker.
- `convert_messages_for_native_relocate_frames_tool_image_as_external_output` — the image is preceded by fixed external-output framing, without copying instruction-shaped tool text into the label.

#10448's default-coupled tests remain updated for the new default (schema round-trip expects `relocate`; `convert_messages_for_native_promotes_tool_result_image_markers` sets `image_url` explicitly; the `omit` tests are unchanged). Local full-workspace build is not possible on the author's box (OOM); hosted CI supplies broader validation. The initial `CI Required Gate` failed because the unrelated `Repository Structure` Apple-preflight test counted a subprocess reap sleep as a retry. #11101 fixes that test on master. [Run 36081372054, attempt 2](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36081372054/attempts/2) passed on c3948b5a927f7b8a6ef2b7d46cc27c847c60c050 after rerunning the failed jobs.

On the refreshed head, the whole gate (fmt, `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`
with `-D warnings`, clippy, and the lib tests) runs green on Linux.

Negative check, as requested: with the `Relocate` arm in `convert_messages_for_native`
made unreachable and nothing else changed, exactly eight tests fail and nothing else
does — the seven relocate tests plus the new default-coverage one:

```
convert_messages_for_native_relocates_tool_result_image_to_user_message
convert_messages_for_native_relocates_tool_result_image_without_setting_the_policy
convert_messages_for_native_merges_tool_image_into_following_user_message
convert_messages_for_native_relocate_labels_each_parallel_call_group
convert_messages_for_native_relocate_does_not_echo_tool_call_id_into_user_text
convert_messages_for_native_relocate_labels_missing_id_groups_by_distinct_ordinal
convert_messages_for_native_relocate_links_image_to_its_producing_call_across_identical_text
convert_messages_for_native_relocate_frames_tool_image_as_external_output
```

So the fixtures reach relocation through the declared `attachments` array, rather
than passing for the wrong reason.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes:** the default moves tool-produced images into a user-role carrier. Fixed external-tool-output labels and matching local ordinals preserve their source association without copying provider IDs or tool-result text into the user label. Image bytes are unchanged. This framing does not guarantee immunity to visual prompt injection.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Behavior change to a default.** The default `tool_result_image_policy` changes from `image_url` to `relocate`; for an image-returning tool result this moves the image from the tool message into a following user message. This is a no-op on providers that never receive image parts, succeeds on endpoints that previously 400'd, and uses a user-message image shape rather than relying on tool-role image support. Anyone who specifically wants the old in-tool shape can set `tool_result_image_policy = "image_url"`. Serialized config still omits the field at its (new) default.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **Additive value + default change** — one new accepted value (`"relocate"`) for the existing `tool_result_image_policy` key, now its default.
- Rust / MSRV / toolchain floor changed? **No**

## Rollback

- **Fast rollback:** revert the single squash commit; the default returns to `image_url`, the `relocate` variant disappears, and any config still naming it falls back to a parse error at that key (resolved by switching to `image_url`/`omit`). No data migration or companion changes.

- **Feature flags or config toggles:** Set `tool_result_image_policy = "image_url"` to retain the previous wire shape, or `"omit"` to drop tool-result images while retaining text.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** an image-returning tool still causes an upstream 400, the model receives no image, or a relocated image is associated with the wrong tool result.

prs.title: feat(plugins): replace an installed package through staged admission
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Stacked on #11236: the update commit is rebased onto #11236's fixes, `ade89c66c5` merged #11236's `9f2af02f72`, and `93f1337146` merges its current head, `7a3ad81ed5`, which merges `master` after #11302 landed. Until #11236 merges, this PR's diff also contains its commits. Please review the update commit, `420969ea90` (`feat(plugins): replace an installed package through staged admission`), and its follow-ups, `284d282048`, `9014776427`, `ef150ebef3`, `c21e06242d` and `369fb21334`; the merge commits only bring in #11236 and `master`.
- **What changed and why:**
  - #10995 asks for `zeroclaw plugin update` with verified replacement and rollback. This PR is the host half; the stacked CLI PR, #11262, builds on it. The contract was posted on the issue for review: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/10995#issuecomment-5894198515. It is built on the package protocol #11236 introduces, so every step that changes the plugins directory runs under the persistent hidden package lock, holds each moved directory generation in a leased hidden transaction, uses no-replace renames where supported, and deletes only through the transaction's own handle. The existing plain-rename fallback remains under the separate source-race hold noted below.
  - `PluginHost::admit_update(name, source)` is `admit_source` with the identity decided the other way round. `name` must be loaded, which is checked before the source is opened. The source's manifest must name it, which `admit_open_directory` checks after the shape check and before the signature check and the component read. Everything else is #11236's admission, unchanged.
  - `PluginHost::update_admitted(admitted)`, under the package lock:
    - stages the replacement in a leased `installing` transaction exactly as `install_admitted` does, then checks the staged skill bundle of a skill-capable package as discovery will: staging copies no symbolic links while admission follows links inside the package, so a bundle admission accepted can stage incomplete. It is refused, with the reason, before the installed package is touched;
    - claims the installed directory into a leased `replacing` transaction and checks that the claimed generation has the manifest text, which carries all the authority the caller compared, and the admitted component this host loaded. A package replaced since with a different manifest or component is published back untouched and the update refused with `NamespaceChanged`. Skill content is not compared; it was never admitted bytes;
    - publishes the replacement into the directory the package was discovered in, by #11236's publication helper. Its no-replace path refuses an existing destination; the plain-rename fallback remains under a separate hold. If that fails, the claimed generation is published back; if even that fails, the new `PluginError::ReplacementInterrupted` names where it is preserved, and its lease is released on return. On every other error the installed package is exactly as it was;
    - gives the replaced generation the delete mark #11236's remove sets once it commits to a delete, then deletes it through its handle, so recovery only ever finishes that delete. One that cannot be deleted stays there, marked, and `ReplacedPackage::leftover` names it.
  - `update_admitted` does not compare authority. Its rustdoc now states the precondition: the caller compares what the replacement requests (permissions, capabilities, `provides` ids and publisher) with the loaded generation and has the operator accept any increase, as #11262's CLI does. What the method guarantees is that the generation it replaces is the one that comparison was made against. An `# Errors` section lists what it returns and what state each leaves. Moving the comparison into the host is #11561.
  - `PluginHost::recover_interrupted_update(name)` covers a process stopped mid-update. Under the lock it judges only `replacing` transactions of `name` whose lease it can take; a held lease is reported as `RecoveryRetained`, and a lookup error inside a claim refuses rather than counting as absence. Whether the package is installed is judged by discovering the plugins directory again under the lock, never from the host's earlier view, which can predate the update that left the claims, and an installed package of the name takes precedence over any claimed generation. When it is installed, every claimed generation is marked for deletion and deleted, and one that cannot be is reported in `UpdateRecovery::Swept.kept`. When it is not, the one restorable claim is published back to `<plugins_dir>/<name>`, so the restored package is admitted only if the configured policy accepts it. Several claims, or anything already at the name, are reported and left as found; a generation marked for deletion is never put back; a claim that holds neither is finished; an empty transaction a stopped process left without a lease is removed, and a non-empty one is reported. Abandoned stages of `name` are swept with #11236's `remove_stale_staging`, and a namespace change refuses. `displaced_packages()`, also under the lock and judging installation the same way, lists the names with an abandoned claim that holds a package.
  - Also: `write_package` writes the admitted component after the `skills/` copy, so a component under `skills/` holds the admitted bytes even if the source changed after admission. One fix of #11236's own scope is carried here because the update work found it: install now runs the same staged skill check, so it refuses a staged bundle discovery would reject instead of publishing a package discovery then skips. Configuration and durable state are untouched: `PluginInstanceId` excludes the version, so the package's `[[plugins.entries]]` rows and state carry over.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No CLI, config, WIT, or on-disk format change beyond one more hidden transaction kind, `replacing`. The one operator-visible change is install's refusal above. The CLI, its Fluent strings, and the operator docs are in #11262.
  - `remove` and discovery behave as in #11236; install does too, except for the `write_package` order and the staged skill check above. `remove` leaves `replacing` transactions alone: the displaced generation of a removed package is put back only by a named update.
  - Renames are not followed by `fsync`, as #11236's install does not fsync either, and the replaced generation is deleted right after the replacement is published. A power loss right after an update may leave the new package partly unflushed with the previous one already gone; #11262's docs give the remedy.
  - Discovery still reads a package's manifest and its component by path at different moments, so a daemon that discovers during a swap can pair the previous manifest with the new component when no `wasm_sha256` binds them, until its next discovery. Admitting discovered packages through one directory handle, as admission already does, is #11562.
  - Staging never follows symbolic links, so a bundle with real skills beside linked ones still installs and updates without the linked ones.
  - A process killed between publishing the replacement and marking the replaced generation for deletion leaves that generation claimed. Recovery deletes it while the package is installed; after a later `plugin remove`, a named update would put it back.
- **Blast radius:** The published `zeroclaw-plugins` API gains `admit_update`, `update_admitted`, `recover_interrupted_update`, `displaced_packages`, `ReplacedPackage`, `UpdateRecovery`, and `PluginError::ReplacementInterrupted`. #11236's exhaustive `is_structural_admission_failure` classifies the variant as non-structural here, since admission never returns it. `host/recovery.rs` gains `transaction_package`, and #11236's delete mark is now shared by remove and update; `LoadedPlugin` keeps its admitted manifest text. Update opens the plugins root on first use, as install and remove do.
  - #11232 has landed on `master`, and #11236 merges `master` after it, so the stack holds one revision of each. `claimed_is_loaded` relies on `admit_component_in`, which #11232 and #11236 moved onto the no-follow walk; the replacement and recovery tests pass on this head. Merge order: #11236, this PR, #11262.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10995 (closed by the stacked CLI PR, #11262). Depends on #11236. Related #7432, #11232. Follow-ups: #11561, #11562.
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `docs`, `dependencies`, `core`, `runtime`, `distinguished contributor`, `release-gate`, `domain:security`, `risk:high`, `size:XL`, `cli`, `ci:windows`, `topic:plugins`, `release:v0.8.6`.

### Since the last reviews

tidux requested changes at `f817e5386e`, which JordanTheJet had approved. Each item:

- **Restack.** The commit is rebased onto #11236's fixes, `c5fbbe2313`, as `420969ea90`, and `89cd78102d` merges #11236's later merge of `master`. The rebase conflicted only in `host/recovery.rs` and `host/recovery_tests.rs`, as your simulated restack showed. The approvals at `f817e5386e` do not cover this head.
- **One delete mark.** `SUPERSEDED` and `Transaction::retire` are gone. Update gives the replaced generation the mark remove sets (`mark_deleting`) and deletes it with `finish_delete`, and recovery classifies a marked claim as one it only ever deletes. The mark's doc comment says what it means for both.
- **Bounded barrier.** #11236's version, which gives up after 30 seconds, is kept, and this commit no longer changes it.
- **One empty-entry rule.** `abandoned_claims` uses `Root::remove_empty_entry`.
- **Tests on the new walk.** The replacement and recovery tests pass on `369fb21334`; see the commands below. Since #11236 now opens the plugins root on first use, update, recovery and `displaced_packages` do too.
- **Authority in the host API.** Documented as a precondition, with an `# Errors` section, on `update_admitted`. Moving the check into the host is tracked in #11561.
- **Mixed manifest and component in discovery.** Tracked in #11562, linked from the scope boundary.
- **`plugin remove` retiring abandoned `replacing` claims.** Not done here. `remove` still leaves `replacing` transactions alone, as the scope boundary says. The window it would close, a stop between publishing and marking, is narrow, and it would make remove act on update's transactions, which I'd rather review on its own.

### What this does, simply

To update a plugin, ZeroClaw has to swap one package directory for another without leaving the operator with no working plugin when the swap fails or the process stops part-way. This PR adds that swap to the plugin host; the command that uses it is the next PR.

The new version is first checked exactly as a fresh install is checked, then written, complete, into a hidden folder. Only then does the host move the installed folder into a hidden folder of its own, check that it is still the version the update was prepared against, and move the new folder into its place. If that move fails, the old folder is moved back.

Every step that changes the plugins folder happens under the same lock install and remove use, so those steps never interleave across processes, and whatever ran before the lock is checked again under it. If the process dies part-way, the hidden folders say how far it got, and the lock on each ends with the process: the next update puts the old version back, or finishes cleaning up. An update and its recovery never delete a package by name.

### Completed-update cache correction

The signed follow-up 284d2820482d3b818e386ad5320654c3b3d49edd fixes a host that loaded a package before another host completed an update and could retain the old generation after all update claims were removed. Recovery now refreshes the installed view under the existing package lock even when no abandoned claims remain. This also removes stale cached packages that another host deleted, while preserving current and missing-package no-op behavior.

The one-file follow-up adds three deterministic host regressions for completed replacement followed by another replacement, external removal while preserving another package, and current/missing-package no-ops. Source and patch/whitespace checks pass. Fresh official Rust, format and lint checks for this follow-up are pending; older green checks do not validate it. No local Rust tests were run.

The current #11236 copy repair still needs normal parent reconciliation before combined qualification and merge. The rename fallback, shared-lock qualification, #11561/#11562, and downstream #11262 config-persistence/token concerns remain separate. This cache correction does not close those holds.

### Since the cache correction

`9014776427` answers the review thread on `displaced_packages`: two calls on one host shared one open lock file, and `flock` does not make a second taker of the same open file wait. `recovery::Root` now also holds an in-process mutex for as long as its lock guard lives, under the same bounded wait. `a_second_thread_sharing_the_root_waits_for_the_package_lock` covers it and fails with the mutex removed.

`ade89c66c5` merges #11236's current head, `9f2af02f72`, which streams skill assets through a bounded buffer and keeps executable helpers' execute bits. The merge was clean and leaves the update commits unchanged.

`ef150ebef3` answers the review thread on batch updates: recovery judged the whole plugins directory again, so `plugin update --all`, which recovers each of its names, admitted every installed package once per name. Recovery now judges again only the package it was asked about. The refresh keeps discovery's loop, because discovery keys a package by its manifest's name and admits neither of two directories that claim one name, and skips each entry whose manifest names another package before anything else about it is checked. `recovery_without_claims_refreshes_only_the_named_package` fails if the no-claims branch rediscovers everything, and `recovery_refresh_admits_neither_package_of_a_name_two_directories_claim` fails if the refresh matches by directory name instead.

`93f1337146` merges #11236's `7a3ad81ed5`, which brings in the 36 `master` commits since `ee79b1f483`, among them #11302. #11302 gives `publish_and_seed_plugin` a channel binding argument, so the stranded-directory install test passes none. The update commits are unchanged.

`c21e06242d` answers the review thread on `--all` putting back a package it never named. A batch takes its names from the host's discovery, so a package an interrupted update displaced after that was still listed, and recovery restored it. `sweep_interrupted_update` is the recovery a batch runs: it deletes what finished updates left, but leaves a claimed package where it is and reports `UpdateRecovery::Displaced`, which it decides under the package lock. `a_sweep_leaves_a_package_displaced_after_discovery_where_it_is` fails if the sweep puts the package back.

`369fb21334` answers the review thread on recovery dropping its cleanup warnings. Recovery deletes the generations finished updates left before it puts a displaced package back, and only a `Swept` outcome reported one it could not delete. `Restored`, `Ambiguous`, `Occupied` and `Displaced` now carry `kept` too, and `UpdateRecovery::kept` returns it for any outcome. `recovery_that_restores_a_package_reports_a_generation_it_cannot_delete` fails if a restoring recovery drops it. The commands below ran on `369fb21334`.

prs.title: fix(sop): match step scope groups to registered tool names
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - The SOP step scope groups `fs`/`filesystem` and `web`/`network` expanded to `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `web_search`. The tool registry registers `file_read`, `file_write`, `file_edit`, and `web_search_tool`. `resolve_excluded` matches expanded group members against registry names, so those four members never matched a tool.
  - With `sop.step_scope_enforce = true`, `deny-tools: fs` removed nothing, `deny-tools: web` removed only `http_request`, and `allow-tools: fs` removed every tool except the mandatory ones. This corrects the four names.
  - `expand_group` now reads one group table, and new tests build the production tool registry and check every group against it, so a renamed tool or a mistyped member fails a test instead of silently disabling a scope.
  - The resolver unit tests in `scope/mod.rs` used a fake registry with the same wrong names, which is why they passed. The fixture now uses real tool names.
  - The registry-building test helper keeps both config arguments in its temp dir, so the test never touches the developer's real `~/.zeroclaw`; the first revision of this PR opened the session store there.
- **Scope boundary:** Group membership is unchanged (see open questions). No change to resolver semantics, SOP parsing, config, schema, or docs. No validation or warning is added for scope entries that match no registered tool. Other tests that use `read_file` as an arbitrary name in their own fake registries are left alone, because they do not go through group expansion.
- **Blast radius:** SOP step turns (live and headless) and child or delegated runs that inherit a step scope, only when `sop.step_scope_enforce = true` and a step's `allow-tools:`, `deny-tools:`, or legacy `tools:` list names `fs`, `filesystem`, `web`, or `network`. Steps that list explicit tool names, and every install with enforcement off (the default), behave as before.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

An SOP step can carry a tool scope: an allow list, a deny list, or both. When an operator turns on `sop.step_scope_enforce`, the runtime removes tools from the step according to that scope. Entries can be tool names or short group names such as `fs` or `web`, which stand for several tools.

The group table spelled four tools differently from how the runtime registers them. A step told to deny `fs` kept its file tools, a step told to deny `web` kept web search, and a step told to allow only `fs` lost every tool except the SOP lifecycle tools that are always kept, including the file tools it asked for.

This PR corrects the four names and adds tests that compare the group table with the tool registry the runtime actually builds.

### Open questions for maintainers

1. **Group membership.** Should `fs`/`filesystem` also cover `glob_search` and `content_search`, and should `web`/`network` also cover `web_fetch`? All three are registered by default. After this fix, `deny-tools: fs` still leaves the local discovery tools `glob_search` and `content_search`, as well as other default tools that touch files, such as `shell`, `git_operations`, `deliver_file`, and `image_info`; `deny-tools: network` still leaves `web_fetch` and any other tool that can reach the network. Changing membership changes what operators get from a group, so it is left out of this fix.
2. **Unmatched scope entries.** A scope entry that matches no group and no registered tool is ignored without a warning, which is how this went unnoticed. Should SOP load or save warn or reject? Note that the tool-call parser accepts `read_file` and similar spellings from models as aliases for `file_read`, which can make those spellings look valid in a scope.
3. **Documentation.** The group names are not in `docs/book/src/sop/syntax.md`. They could be documented once membership is settled.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`. No interface changes, and the new unit tests run the resolver against the production tool registry.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The Rust test jobs run the `zeroclaw-runtime` lib tests, which include the new `sop::scope::groups::tests`. The Lint, Format, and compile-check jobs cover the two changed files.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The advisory Windows test lane did not run for this diff, and `Check x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` runs `cargo check` without test targets, so the new tests have not been compiled or run on Windows; that job covers only the non-test change. No group member name is platform-specific.
- **Commands run and tail output:** macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64), rustc 1.97.1, at commit `3a73f5f7a9` (the test-only follow-up on top of `1452eaaba8`; the same commands gave the same results on `1452eaaba8`). Cargo commands ran with `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=0 CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG=0` to keep the build small.

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib sop::scope
running 8 tests
test sop::scope::tests::mandatory_infra_survives_empty_allow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::allow_scope_excludes_everything_else ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::security_policy_can_only_narrow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::mandatory_infra_cannot_restore_policy_denied_tools ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::every_group_member_is_a_registered_tool_name ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::denying_a_group_excludes_exactly_its_registered_tools ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::allowing_a_group_keeps_exactly_its_registered_tools ... ok

test result: ok. 8 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5309 filtered out; finished in 0.03s
exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib sop
test result: ok. 793 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 4523 filtered out; finished in 6.31s
exit=0

$ printf '%s\0' crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/scope/groups.rs crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/scope/mod.rs > files.nul
$ python3 scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.py files.nul
Comment hygiene gate passed.
exit=0

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
error: unused import: `std::sync::mpsc`
  --> crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:15:5
error: could not compile `zeroclaw-runtime` (lib test) due to 1 previous error
exit=101

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings -A unused_imports
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 1m 29s
exit=0
```

The strict clippy failure is in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs`, which this PR does not touch. On this PR's base the import is gated `#[cfg(any(windows, test))]` while its only test use is gated `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`, so it is unused in macOS test builds only; a warn-only clippy run over all targets reports that one diagnostic and none in `sop/scope/`. Master already gates the import correctly (PR 11314). With origin/master `f12da7462a` merged into this branch locally, the same command exits 0:

```text
# local merge of origin/master f12da7462a into 3a73f5f7a9
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib sop::scope
test result: ok. 8 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5718 filtered out; finished in 0.03s
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 1m 04s
exit=0
```

The registry-building tests also ran with an empty temporary `HOME` and no `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR`:

```text
$ HOME=<empty temp dir> target/debug/deps/zeroclaw_runtime-<hash> sop::scope::groups
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5314 filtered out; finished in 0.02s
(nothing was created under that HOME)
```

The new tests fail without the fix. At `3a73f5f7a9` with the four names reverted to `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `web_search`:

```text
test sop::scope::tests::deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::denying_a_group_excludes_exactly_its_registered_tools ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::every_group_member_is_a_registered_tool_name ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::allowing_a_group_keeps_exactly_its_registered_tools ... FAILED

assertion `left == right` failed: deny scope `fs`
  left: []
 right: ["edit_file", "read_file", "write_file"]

scope group ["fs", "filesystem"] lists `read_file`, which the test registry did not register: fix the name, or switch on its config gate in registered_tool_names()

test result: FAILED. 4 passed; 4 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5309 filtered out; finished in 0.04s
```

`deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow` fails there because its fixture now uses real names and expands `fs`. With only `web_search_tool` reverted to `web_search`:

```text
assertion `left == right` failed: deny scope `web`
  left: ["http_request"]
 right: ["http_request", "web_search"]

scope group ["web", "network"] lists `web_search`, which the test registry did not register: fix the name, or switch on its config gate in registered_tool_names()
```
